maintopic: PRIVILEGE-REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
PRIVILEGE-REPRESENTATION OF QUEBEC EAST AND OTTAWA.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) yesterday, (December 1), called my attention, as 27
a matter of privilege, to the position of another hon. member of this House who had been returned for two constituencies and had not yet declared or elected for which of the two constituencies he would continue to retain his seat.
The contention was made that a certain sessional order of the House of Commons of Great Britain, requiring a member under such circumstances if within one week that it should be made to appear that there was no question as to his return, &c., was applicable to the case referred to inasmuch as such a case was not provided for by the rules and orders of this House. Rule No. 1 of this House is as follows;
In all cases not provided for hereinafter or by sessional or other orders, the rules, usages and forms of proceeding of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in force on the first day of July, 1867, shall be followed.
In the imperial parliament the matter under consideration is dealt with by sessional orders which are renewed by the House of Commons from session to session and which expire at prorogation.
The sessional order on the subject which was, presumably, passed by the imperial House in 1867 may or may not have been in force on the first day of July in that year depending on whether the House was then in session or had been prorogued before that date. Even if that sessional order was in force _ on the first day of July, 1867, the question as to whether that order in all its terms is applicable to the House of Commons of Canada is one of importance and not without difliculty. As far as I have been able to ascertain in the limited time allowed me since the question was raised, I have not been able to find that it has been observed in this country. In fact, from a somewhat hasty consideration of the precedents, I think I would be safe in saying that the practice of this House as to the time in which the member's choice shall be made, has been far from uniform and to the present time no formal ruling on the subject has been made in this House.
The question is, are such sessional orders as are annually passed by the British House of Commons at the beginning of each session included in the meaning of the words ' rules, usages and forms of proceeding ' mentioned in rule 1 of this House. Those sessional orders are clearly neither rules nor forms of proceeding nor in the strict meaning of the term are they to be considered 1 usages ' and consequently are not applicable to this House in cases not specifically provided for. The practice of this House has so far not recognized them as binding.
In 1873, Hon. Mr. Blake having been elected for Durham and Bruce announced his choice of constituency fifteen days after



the beginning of the session, and in 1896 Mr. Dalton McCarthy elected which of the two seats (Brandon and Simcoe) he would sit for, on the seventh day after the opening of the session. The case of the honourable the present Postmaster General, returned for both Nicolet and Gaspe in 1904, is one of the latest in point. He only resigned for Nicolet on the third of December, 1906, and after some fifteen months had elapsed during which he might have exercised his privilege of choice. No doubt a search of the journals and records would show many similar cases.
A strict adherence to the British rule would therefore to a certain extent form an alteration in the customs and usages of this House in that regard.
My ruling is, therefore, that there is nothing in the rule of this House requiring a member who has been returned for more than one constituency to elect within any prescribed time for which of such constituencies he will sit. But, in my opinion, it is eminently desirable that some definite rule and practice on the subject should be established. The House has a Standing Committee for the purpose of considering such questions-the Committee on Privileges and Elections-and I would suggest that at an early date the matter should be considered by the House, or by the committee, with a view to the fixing of a definite period within which such election is to be made.

Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I desire to call the attention of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth) to a matter of considerable importance to a portion of the constituency which I represent. It is stated that a man named William J. Kelly, living in Richmond, in the county of Carleton, N.B., has been kidnapped by United States officers and is now incarcerated in gaol in Portland, in the State of Maine. Of course, of this I have no proofs such as might be required in a court of law, but I have sufficient evidence in my hands to convince me that the man has been kidnapped. The circumstances of the case are as follows:

I do not think that the hon. gentleman is permitted at this stage to go beyond a question except with the indulgence of the House. Of course there will be a motion later on, at which time this subject may be brought up.

It is my intention only to ask a question. It seems that about seven years ago this man was one night teaming a load of produce into the United States and was confronted by a gentleman who turned out to be a United States officer.
That is a positive statement.

I cannot make the matter plain to ask a question without laying some little foundation for it. The result was that the United States officer fired on this man Kelly twice, one bullet taking effect in his cheek and another striking a buckle on a belt which he wore. Kelly seized a stick and in the end the officer was laid out and Kelly returned to his own side of the line. That was seven years ago. About three weeks ago a gentleman came to Kelly's residence in Richmond and wanted to buy some produce from him. Kelly succeeded in selling him some produce at a good price. Then the man wanted him to haul it to the United States but Kelly refused to do so. However, after considerable dickering, he agreed to take it to the boundary line. They started in the evening and came to a place called Union Corners where for about a quarter of a mile the highway road is, for all practical purposes, the boundary line. They had proceeded along this line 30 or 40 rods when a number of men appeared on the scene and Kelly was arrested, gagged, and carried off into the Mr. BRADBURY,
United States. I am satisfied that the boundary line is at least 3 or 4 rods to the west of the point where Kelly was arrested. He is now incarcerated in gaol in Portland and I would like to know if the government have any information on the subject and if they have if they will give it to the House. Will they do whatever is possible in order to have this man set at liberty and to see that the rights of British Subjects are not thus interfered with by American officers?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter to which my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) has called attention is certainly one of very grave importance and one which will be, I have no doubt, on its being brought to the attention of the government of the United States, given the most careful consideration. I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) that in a very general way the facts to which he has referred were a few days ago brought to my attention in the shape of a letter from a gentleman of the vicinity who stated in substance what my hon. friend has just stated to this House. I replied immediately, pointing out the necessity for the most careful accuracy in regard to the particulars of such an allegation, the importance of establishing, as definitely and certainly as evidence could establish such a fact, just where upon this highway, the actual arrest of Kelly took place and also, if it was possible to establish it, whether or not the men who arrested him and carried him into the United States were officers authorized by any competent authority of either the federal or state government. I have not yet received any answer to the request for this information and until it is supplied in definite form and supported by the ordinary verification of affidavit or statutory declaration, we should hardly he in a position to ask the government of the United States to investigate the matter. But as soon as we are placed in possession of the necessary evidence in that regard, I shall see that steps are taken to bring it to the attention of His Majesty's representative in Washington and through him to that of the United States government.
Such cases as this, I may say, do occasionally arise, possibly from the over-zeal of officers upon either side of the boundary. Occasionally a complaint is received that the sacred soil of the United States has been violated by some Canadian officer and similar cases, such as the hon. gentleman has mentioned, sometimes have been shown to exist where some officer of the United States has undertaken to execute his warrant upon the soil of Canada, which I need not say is equally sacred and which I am sure the government of the United States desires to preserve as equally sacred with their own. There has never been any

difficulty put in the way of the most careful and thorough investigation of such charges when they are made, and if it can be established that in point of actual fact this man was deprived of his liberty while upon the soil of Canada, I think I can confidently assure my hon. friend that the fullest reparation will be made by the restoration of the man to Canadian soil.
I did not catch to whom the minister had applied for information with reference to this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I applied to the gentleman whose letter I had received, a clergyman of the vicinity. I think his name was the Rev. Father Murphy, although I am not certain.
Not through any legal source?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not a lawyer, a clergyman.

Before the orders of the day are called, I wish to ask the government a question with reference to the courtesy due or which should be due the representatives of foreign nations in Canada as a country making her own treaties. My question is founded on an article which I now have before me from the daily ' Free Press,' which reads:
All the Consuls stayed away from it-Drawing Room sees them not because of the
ruling of Downing Street.
None of the foreign Consuls General resident in Ottawa attended the Governor General's ' Drawing Room ' on Saturday night.
There is a reason and an interesting one.
Consuls General have no official status in Canada-they are not officially recognized.
When a new Consul General comes to Ottawa, no official calls are made upon him. He has to paddle around in his own canoe and trust to his own ingenuity in getting acquainted.
A Consul General is the highest official that any foreign country can send to Canada. If they could, some of them would doubtless send ambassadors.
The recent establishment of a Chinese consulate in Ottawa, with a gentleman of very high standing in his own country in charge, was regarded by Canadians as a pleasing development of our nationality. It was a recognition of Canada's growing importance.
It has been said that Germany and France are both desirous of establishing Consuls General in Ottawa. But in the case of each, there is reason to believe that the refusal to grant official status stands in the way.
Although the Consuls General at present resident in Ottawa refuse to discuss the matter, the ' Free Press ' understands that it is for the same reason that none of them attend the Drawing Room.
They do not demand recognition; they do not even ask for it; but they do take the
ground that they cannot permit their respective countries to be discriminated against in Canada's official functions. Consequently they absent themselves.
The official order of precedence at the Drawing Room, published in the newspapers, places the Consuls General at the very end of the list.	_	_ _
In refusing official recognition the Dominion is acting upon definite instructions received from Downing street.
But Cahada's natural reply to this would be that England is able to show official courtesy to these foreign countries by recognizing their Ambassadors, whereas the foreign governments are not permitted to send Ambassadors to Canada.
No general instructions to colonial governors respecting the position and treatment of consuls appear to have been issued since a date nearly forty years ago, when it was intimated that if in any colony precedence was, as a matter of courtesy, already accorded to the foreign consular body, no alteration should be made, with the view of assimilating the practice to that in force in this country, without reference to the Secretary of State.
It was observed, however, that foreign consuls in England have no claim to precedency, and are treated like any other foreigners resident in England.
Toronto ' Daily Star,' Monday, Nov. 8, 1909. r Ambassador from Germany '-New Consulate General at Ottawa to be a Big Thing.
(Canadian Associated Press.)
London, Eng., Nov. 10.-The Canadian Associated Press learns that the German government is considering the advisability of establishing a new Consulate General at Ottawa, which will be almost ambassadorial in its scope, character, and plans. Already plans have been suggested for the erection of a building.
The imperial army and navy recognize officially consuls in every foreign port. Why should not this be in our own country? I wish to ask the right hon. gentleman if any steps have been taken to remedy this state of affairs under a ruling which was made under different conditions. When we had not the power of making our own treaties; and if the government have not taken any steps, I should like to know whether they intend doing something. The consuls general are in Canada the highest representatives of foreign states, and while the matter of attending the drawing room may be, to a certain extent, a small one, still when we consider that the important question as to the size of a lady's foot occasioned a war which consumed millions of money and thousands of lives, this matter may not seem to be one which should be lightly treated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The question which my hon. friend has brought to our attention is an important one, not perhaps so much on account of the drawing room as on account of the duties which consuls general now discharge in Canada. We have

no diplomatic service in Canada, and the consuls general are exercising by tolerance some, I shall not say diplomatic powers, but powers very often cognate to such. The question is one which should be settled, and the matter is now engaging the attention of the government.

Can the right hon. gentleman give any information as to when the Naval Bill will be introduced? I think there is an impression that we were to have a statement from my right hon. friend regarding that matter on some occasion previous even to the present.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thought that we would have been in a position to introduce the Bill 'ere this, but my hon. friend himself has called attention to certain correspondence which it will be desirable to have. We have not yet received that correspondence, and perhaps -we would be better to wait until we receive it before bringing down the measure.
May we expect it next week?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I could not say definitely, but have no intention to delay the Bill, and will bring it down as soon as we get the correspondence.

Why should this correspondence interfere with bringing down the Bill? Two weeks ago the right hon. gentleman said the Bill w'ould be introduced soon. He knows that it will have to be printed, which will take some days. Is that correspondence going to affect the Bill? If not, why not bring down the Bill and give hon. members a chance to study it before taking any action on it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) asked for some information, which I supposed would be valuable to the members of the opposition and also to the government.

Why should that interfere with bringing down the Bill. I understood that the Bill was practically all ready some two weeks ago. If it is ready, the House is entitled to have the Bill immediately, and that need not interfere with the bringing down of the correspondence. The correspondence may be brought down afterwards and be made use of during the discussion. Does the right hon. gentleman refuse to introduce the Bill until we have the correspondence ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the correspondence is to be unduly delayed, we shall not wait for it. I do not think it will affect my own judgment, but I see no harm in having the correspondence before we give our decision. .

MILLER (South Grey) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 6) to amend the Criminal Code. He said: Mr. Speaker, before going into the discussion of this Bill, let me now, lest I forget it, give notice that, when the House is in committee on this Bill, I will move the following:
That the said Bill be amended by adding the following as paragraph (e) to section 230:-
Being the owner or other person in control of premises occupied or used as a disorderly house, knowingly allows any contrivance whatsoever upon the said premises for the purpose of preventing, obstructing or delaying the entry of any constable or officer authorized as aforesaid into any such disorderly house of any part thereof.
The reason for that amendment is that it is complained by constables and police officers that, in seeking to inspect or gain entry to Chinese gambling houses in many cases, they find that the occupants of the house have their inner rooms barricaded with very stout doors, thus preventing the police from gaining entry until the inmates have had an opportunity to escape.
In discussing the Bill itself, I wish first to state what is the object of the Bill. Its object is to utterly, entirely, completely suppress and prevent the business of betting, pool-making, book-making, the busi-

ness of betting or gambling in connection with or upon race tracks in any place in Canada. If the Bill should become law and fail of its object, it will be because the persons who have laboured to produce the Bill have not been able to find language that will accomplish the objec.t. they have in view. And I desire, at the beginning of my remarks, to say that I do not claim the credit, if credit be due to any person, for the framing of the Bill that is now before the House. The Bill that we are "considering is based upon the work of three well known and able members of the legal profession. At least two of the three gentlemen upon whose very careful work the Bill is based have had peculiar experience and occupy positions that have made it possible for them with special ability to frame a law to meet the evils that we are endeavouring to combat. I have stated the object of the Bill; now let me state as frankly what the Bill does not endeavour to do. I want to impress the House with this, that the Bill does not endeavour to interfere in any way or to any extent with the racing of horses. Men will be just as free after this Bill becomes law to race horses or carry on a race meet as they are to-day or ever have been. Neither does this Bill seek to prevent betting upon horse races. If this Bill becomes law, two men will be just as free to make a bet upon which horse will win a race as they will to make a bet upon which of themselves can throw a stone the greater distance. The Bill does not, then, endeavour to affect horse-racing or to prevent betting between private individuals in connection with horse-racing, and I trust that every one who hears me will bear that in mind. Neither is it the endeavour by this legislation to correct any past bungling on the part of this parliament. I say that because many people have had the idea that the present state of the law, which appears to them absurd, is the result of error or lack of skill on the part of legislators of the past. One prominent Ontario newspaper, in a somewhat recent editorial, said:
The Department of Justice has failed so far bo frame a statute that will do what parliament manifestly intended should be done.
Very many people have had that opinion, but the opinion is an erroneous one. Parliament has never, up to this time, endeavoured to prohibit the 'business of betting or gambling upon race-tracks. Quite the contrary is the case, as I will endeavour to show. And I trust the House will pardon me if I take a little time-I shall not be long-to trace the history of the legislation that we have at present and that people have endeavoured to use to suppress race-track gambling.
Several years ago, men in Canada began to recognize the growing evil of race-track
gambling, the business of race-track betting. This was not so much because public opinion has changed-partly, perhaps, for that reason and because, it may be, we demand to-day a somewhat higher standard than we did a few years ago -but more largely because circumstances in Canada have been changing. Racetrack gambling is much more prevalent to-day than it was in Canada a few yeers ago. There are more race horses in the Dominion, race meets are held for a great deal longer time, and the book-maker is doing a work to-day that he did not attempt to do ten or fifteen years ago, that is, to anything like the same extent. I say that the people realized some years ago the grave evils attending race-track gambling. With that realization they turned to the statutes we had then and have now to see by what means they could suppress or prevent this gambling. They turned to the Criminal Code, section 235-which was section 204 of the Code as first passed in 1892. They found that to be the only section of the Code making reference to race-track gambling. That section, under paragraph (a) provides that every one is liable to the punishment inflicted by the section who uses or knowingly allows any part of any premises under his control to be used for the purpose of recording or registering any bet or wager, or selling any pool. Now that section might probably have been used with considerable effect to suppress. racetrack gambling- had not it been that attached to the section as subsection 2 was the following:
The provisions of this section shall not extend to any person by reason of his becoming the custodian or depository of any money, property, or valuable thing, to be paid as a prize to the winner of any lawful race, sport, game or exercise, or to be paid to the owner of any horse engaged in any lawful race, or to bets between individuals or made on the race course of any incorporated association during the actual progress of a race meeting.
Now, this language in section 235 does not appear to have been inserted in error. In order to show that it was deliberately placed there, let me refer to the remarks of Sir John Thompson and others which will be found in the 'Hansard' of 1892, page 2976. In 1892, as hon. members of the House are aware, the Criminal Coda was first placed upon the statute-book. When the House was in committee considering this section 235, Sir John Thompson said:
I suppose it is my duty to call the attention of the committee to the addition of subsection 2, which proposes a relaxation in regard to betting on the race course of an incorporated association while a race is going on.
So, Sir John Thompson frankly said that this was a relaxation of the law in connection with race-track betting. And Mr.- now Sir Louis Davies said:

It is just as well that the committee should understand that we are legalizing betting on a race course. I do not know that the committee is prepared to do that.
Then Mr. Curran said in reply:
The law has always allowed hetting on horse races.
The matter was allowed to drop, and the section was passed, and included in the Code as we have it before us to-day. Then these people who, rightly or wrongly, were endeavouring some years ago to restrict race-track gambling, finding that section 235 was of no avail, turned to sections 225, 227 and 228 which, in the Criminal Code of 1892, are sections 196, 197 and 198. These sections were not supposed to relate to the restriction of race-track betting at all and an endeavour so to use them was only due to the absence of any legislation intended or enacted for such purpose. Section 235, to which I have already referred, had been in the criminal law of Canada for some years before 1892, but the addition exempting race-track gambling during the course of a meet on a race-track association, was inserted in 1892. But the sections 226, 227 and 228 had not been previously in our criminal law, they were adopted in 1892 from the English Betting Act. Without wearying the House by reading sections 226 and 227, I may say that section 226 defines a common gaming house,
227	defines a common betting house, and
228	imposes the penalty for persons who are guilty of a breach of 226 and 227. Sec-227 reads as follows:
A common betting house is a house, office, room or other place opened, kept or used for the purpose of betting between persons resorting thereto.
I will not read the remainder of the section, but that is the part of it that was relied upon to suppress race-track gambling, and it was the only section, together with the following one, imposing a penalty, that would be of any use, or could possibly be of any use, to bring about the object in view. Somewhere about 1906, I think it was, a man named Saunders, and some companions, were carrying'on the business of book-makers during a meet of the Ontario Jockey Club in the city of Toronto. Complaint was laid against them for keeping a common betting house. They were convicted before the police magistrate of Toronto, and convicted under these sections, 226 and 227. They appealed from his decision, and at their request he stated a case, and it was taken to the Ontario Court of Appeal. The Court of Appeal upheld the magistrate in his decision. Judges Garrow and Meredith, however, dissented, and were of the opinion that the conviction of the magistrate ought to be quashed. The solicitors acting for the defendants in that Mr. MILLER.
case, argued that Saunders and his companions, while they used a booth upon castors which moved from one part of the racetrack to the other, could not be said to be using a house, room or other place as defined by the Act; and if it were held otherwise that they were using such house, room or other place, under section 235 they were exempt, because they did what they did on a race-track of a regularly incorporated racing association. The Court of Appeal, as I have already said, notwithstanding these arguments, upheld the magistrate in his decision. Judges Garrow and Meredith dissented from the other judges, and Judge Garrow said:
The proper construction in a word is in my opinion to bold that sections 197 and 198 (now sections 226 and 227) have no application to the case of betting carried on upon the race course of an incorporated association during the actual progress of a race meeting, whether or not such hetting takes place within or without doors, or in any particular ' house, office, room or other place/ so long as it is within the boundaries of the race course and so long as the betting is confined to the races in progress upon that race course.
That was the view of Judge Garrow. But the Court of Appeal having sustained the magistrate in his decision, the case was carried to the Supreme Court. The judges of the Supreme Court confirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeal, and in upholding the magistrate here again two judges dissented from their brother judges and gave their opinion. Mr. Justice Davies and Mr. Justice Girouard differed from the other judges of the Supreme Court. Chief Justice Fitzpatrick, in delivering judgment, said:
I quite agree that the amendment of 1892 was intended to reserve the race courses of incorporated associations as places where bets might he recorded and registered, and any apparatus or structures used for more conveniently recording such bets or wagers, provided this was done during the actual progress of a race meeting, were exempted from the operation of that section.
But using a place for the purpose of recording or registering bets or wagers is something entirely different from using the place for the purpose of hetting between persons resorting thereto and the owner or occupier thereof.
Chief Justice Fitzpatrick was drawing a nice distinction between the language of sections 227 and 235. Section 235 says that a penalty is imposed upon any person who uses or knowingly allows any part of any premises under his control to be used for the purpose, not of betting, but of recording or registering any bet or wager. Section 227, on the other hand, imposes a penalty on any person who has opened, kept or used a place for the purpose of betting between persons resorting thereto. The one relates

to betting, the other to recording and registering a bet. Drawing this distinction, Chief Justice Fitzpatrick said:
Bets between individuals or bets made on the race course of an incorporated association during the actual progress of a race meeting can be recorded in any place used for that purpose, but to keep a place, whether within or without the grounds of a racing association for the purpose of betting, whether during the progress of a race meeting or not, is an offence under section 197. In my opinion two distinct and separate statutory offences are created by sections 197 and 201, and that which may be invoked successfully as a defence in one case cannot avail in the other. To keep a place for making bets which may be recorded at that place or elsewhere and to keep a place for recording bets wherever made are distinct and separate acts, each of which has been made an offence and. each of which is declared to subject the offenders to a different penalty. The exception created by subsection 2 of section 201 with respect to anything therein, does not apply to those places that are kept for the purpose of betting. I do not understand the rule of construction to be that all the sections of the Code dealing with nuisances are to be read together to see how they can be made to harmonize any more than the sections dealing with offences against the person or against property. Distinct and separate acts are by these sections declared to be common nuisances and the only question to be considered is: Do the facts proved in evidence support that charge as laid in each particular case? The appeal is dismissed with costs.
Mr. Justice Davies quoted the words of Judge Garrow as given in the Court of Appeal. Nevertheless the Court of Appeal decided to uphold the decision of the magistrate. The result of that decision in the Saunders case was this: That a man who used any structure, any house, office, room or other place, including a booth or other such thing which might be designated as a place was subject to the penalties imposed by that section 227. That, then, perhaps, for a time, cheeked the business of race-track gambling, but some time after that a man named Moylett, a book-maker, with his companions at the Woodbine track in Toronto, continued the very same business of race-track gambling which had been done by Saunders, only, in place of having a booth or tent that moved about, they simply stood on the ground within a limited area, walking from place to place and carrying on exactly the same kind of business. A complaint was made against them and the police magistrate, under the same section of the Code, convicted them of keeping a common betting place. Then Moylett appealed, as Saunders had done and tthe police magistrate as he had done in the other case, granted a stated case which was taken to the Court of Appeal. In this case the Court of Appeal quashed the conviction of the magistrate and Chief Justice Moss, in giving judgment, said:
The defendants and their assistants did not use any desk, stool, umbrella, tent or booth, or erection of any kind to mark any place where bets were made.
He continued:
Viewed apart from the authorities by which we are bound, the words themselves seem almost naturally to suggest a structure of some sort, and to import fixity or localization.
They also import rights peculiar to the persons designated as the owner, occupier or keeper, which rights are not shared by others. It is obvious that there must be not only a house, office, room or other place, but it must be one capable of being opened, kept or used for the purpose of betting. And there must also be some person who is entitled to exercise the right of opening, keeping or using to the exclusion of the exercise of a similar right by others except with his permission.
He said, in conclusion:
But, whatever doubts might possibly have existed before the decision of the House of Lords in the leading case of Powell vs. The Kempton Park Race Course Company (1899) must now be considered as set at rest by the result of that case.
The Kempton Park case, which ruled in this case, was under the English Betting Act where the language used was almost exactly the same as the language in sections 226 and 227 of our own Code and the judges held that the evidence of the facts in the one case corresponded almost exactly with the facts in the other case. In the Kempton Park case Judge Escher said:
It is not betting, whatever be its kind, which, independent of locality, is struck at; but it is the preventing of a locality for particular kinds of betting which is the mischief to be dealt with.
Again, Judge Halsbury said:
The legislature has not prohibited betting at all; but prohibited keeping a house for betting.
Chief Justice Moss, in giving judgment in the Moylett case, said:
If the user of any place where the better happens to stand, makes the place a common betting house, the words ' house, office or room ' were unnecessary, and the words ' other places ' therefore, necessarily take their colour and meaning from the words which precede them, and must be construed as meaning a place ejusdem generis, e. g. a booth, tent, etc., or otherwise equally clearly defined and capable of being used as the former.
The effect of this decision was that a man carrying on the business of race-track gambling would be practically exempt from the operation of the statute if he kept mov-

ing about, upon the ground and was not occupying any fixture such as a tent, booth or anything of that kind within which or upon which to carry on his business. I quote further words from the judgment of Chief Justice Moss. He summed the matter up in this way:
Betting or the business of a book-maker, whether carried on upon a race course or else-w he re, is not prohibited by the Act. If the legislature intends to prohibit it, it is easy for it to say so. It is the opening, keeping or using a common batting house which is penalized.
Let me repeat his words. He said:
If the legislature intends to prohibit it it is easy for it to say so.
The facts appear to have been as stated by Chief Justice Moss that this parliament never intended to prohibit race-track gambling, and if it be true that it is parliament's intention to prohibit race-track gambling it is easy for it to say so. If race-track gambling is an evil, if it is something that ought to be suppressed, it becomes the duty of this parliament to suppress it and the whole responsibility rests upon this parliament. What we seek to do by this Bill is to amend sections 226, 227, 228 and 235 of the Criminal Code which were never intended to suppress race-track gambling and to change them so as to make them effective, so that they will utterly and completely prevent and suppress the business of gambling upon or in connection with a race track. Now I will point out the changes that we seek to make in the Act as it is. Turning to section 226 of the Code which defines a ' common gaming house ' we strike out the word ' house ' and define not a ' common gaming house ' but a ' common gaming place '. We strike out the words ' a house, room or ' and leave simply the word ' place,' so that the section will read a ' place used by any person for gaming, betting ' etc. Turning to Stroud's Judicial Dictionary, an English work, Stroud defines the word ' place ' in this way:
The word ' place ' is generally found in conjunction with other words which give it a colour, and it is usually controlled by its context.
Referring to the words ' house, office, room or other place ' in the English Betting Act he quotes Judge Channell in Brown vs. Patch as follows:
The statute is directed against betting places, not against betting persons.
We are now endeavouring to make the statute apply to betting persons as well as to betting places. Wherever the words * house, room or ' appear in section 226 they are struck out and simply the word ' place ' is left. I have no doubt that the Mr. MILLER.
person who drafted this section intended and endeavoured by the use of this collection of words to make the language more comprehensive, but what he really did was to make the language narrower in effect rather than broader, less comprehensive rather than more so. In section 227 we strike out the words * house, room or ' and leave the one word ' place ' again, and in place of. defining ' any betting house ' we define ' any betting place '. There is another important change in section 227. We add as subsection 2 of this section a definition of the word ' place ' wherever it occurs in the Act.
The word ' place ' as used in this section and in the preceding section, includes any place, whether inclosed or not, whether it is or is not a fixed place, and whether there is or is not an exclusive right of user.
This, then, will do away with the argument that a man standing on the ground is not occupying a place. Section 228, which imposes the penalty, has also the word ' house ' struck out and the word ' place ' substituted therefor. The words ' or other disorderly place ' are inserted after the words ' disorderly house'. Section 232 is amended in the same way to make it consistent with the others. Turning to section 235-and perhaps this section is the most important of any-three important new paragraphs are added to this section the first paragraph of which section defines the penalty which is imposed, that is to say, that every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to one year's imprisonment and to a fine not exceeding $1,000. These new sections are as follows:
(d)	Engages in pool selling or book-making or in the business or occupation of betting or wagering or makes any agreement for the purchase or sale of betting or gaming privileges.

Now, Sir, it may be asked why we seek to amend the law at all, or what necessity there is for the Bill I have introduced. Sir, I am willing to admit that one of the reasons why it has been thought proper to introduce this Bill is because it has been asked for by the Moral and Social Reform Council of Canada. And, whom does this association include? It represents the Church of England in Canada, the Presby-

terian Church, the Methodist Church, the Baptist Church, the Congregational Church, the Salvation Army, the Canadian Purity Educational Association, the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the Dominion Grange and Farmers' Association. I have heard it said that no layman has asked for this legislation, that it is a movement upon the part of the ministers, and that the ministers are not practical men and have no knowledge of the subject. But, Sir, let me say that at the various conferences, synods, presbyteries and meetings of the various churches in Canada resolutions have been unanimously passed urging this government to support just such a Bill as we have now before us, and a large number of the men attending these associations have been laymen, business men, men of the world, men having a knowledge of the subject they were considering and which they have asked this House to consider. But if it be contended that these people have been unduly influenced, it may be by the impractical clergy, let me say that legislation similar to that which I now propose has been passed by the following states: New Mexico, Missouri, Illinois, Washington, South Carolina, Colorado, Texas, New Jersey, Ohio, Virginia, Alabama, Arkansas, Massachusetts, West Virginia, Michigan, Louisiana, California and New York, and the last four of these states are among the greatest horse-breeding states in the American union. I take it that the very fact that this legislation has been passed by this large number of the states of the union is an evidence to us of the necessity of such legislation. I say that because these various states, perhaps without exception, have had a greater, wider, longer experience with race-track gambling than we have had in Canada. These states of the American union have not hitherto been .supposed by the Canadian people to live up to any higher moral standard than we live up to. They are not supposed to aim at any higher moral plane than we should aspire to, but these states have practical business reasons for passing the legislation such as we have before us now. I not only ask the House to take this as evidence of the necessity for the legislation, but I ask hon. gentlemen to consider the effect upon Canada and the Canadian people of .the passing of this prohibitory legislation Toy the various states. The effect has been to flood Canada with American book-makers. Prevented from carrying on their business in these several states they have come into our Dominion with the result that racetrack gambling is much more prevalent in Canada now than it would have been had it not been for this prohibitory law on the other side of the line. Recently a grand jury assembled in Toronto declared that the province of Ontario had become a para-28
dise for gambling. That -was not the verdict of an assembly of clergymen, but the verdict of a grand jury. And, if the prov ince of Ontario has become a paradise for gambling, it is not alone among the provinces; because the province of British Columbia is fast becoming cursed by racetrack gambling, and if there be no change in the law, so soon as our prairie provinces have greater population and greater wealth they will be afflicted with the same curse. I have said that race-track gambling is becoming a nuisance in the province of British Columbia. I was speaking a few days ago with a very prominent citizen of (Victoria, British Columbia, and he told me that race-track gambling had become alarmingly prevalent in that city, and a great evil. An editorial in a Victoria daily newspaper, shortly after the holding of a recent race meet in that city, said that the racing was not true horseracing, but racing of horses as an excuse for gambling. The board of trade of the city of Vancouver, after the holding of a recent race meet in that city, adopted a resolution urging this government to pass such legislation as I am now asking the House to pass. Not only that, but Japan has legislated against race-track gambling. We cannot say that the population of Japan are a goody-goody people, but we can say that perhaps more than any other nation in the world to-day, Japan realizes that the strength of a nation 'depends upon the strength of the individual citizens, and if Japan has passed legislation to do away with race-track gambling, it is because Japan wants to have virtuous citizens and to build up a strong people. I have received a letter from Chief Inspector Archibald, of the Toronto police force, and he manifests a great deal of interest in the legislation which is now before the House. In this letter, dated the 16th of last month, he says:
I would respectfully call your attention io subsection 2 of section 235 of the Criminal Code which you will observe has given colour of right and is in the main responsible for the present undesirable conditions; hence the necessity to expunge this subsection from the statute absolutely.
That is what we are endeavouring to do. Now, Sir, for economic reasons, from the point of view of dollars and cents, it behooves us to pass this legislation. The Toronto ' Telegram ' of the fifth of June last describes what took place during the race meeting which was held in the city of Toronto shortly before that date. The Toronto ' Telegram ' said that at the Woodbine the race meeting had lasted last spring for thirteen days, that on the first day there were 72 book-makers on the track and that for the remaining 12 days of the meet there were from 50 to 80 book-makers present each



day. It said that not more than eight or ten of them were from the city of Toronto, the rest being from outside. And the * Telegram ' went on to say that, as I have before stated, the legislation recently enacted in all these states of the American Union had very much increased race-track gambling within this Dominion. Coming to the matter of dollars and cents, The ' Telegram ' said, not as its opinion, not as an estimate but as a fact, that during that 13 days of the race meeting on the Woodbine our people had placed in the hands of bookmakers $2,600,000 or $200,000 a day for 13 consecutive days.

Mr.' MILLER. It is indeed the growing time, but the growth is the wrong way. The Toronto ' Telegram ' further says it cost these book-makers to be on the ground $115,000. I ask whether it is a desirable state of things that anything [DOT] should induce or be permitted to induce people, most of whom cannot afford it, to place $2,600,000 in 13 days in the custody of American book-makers.
There are many people who appear to fear that if this Bill becomes law it will interfere in some way with Canadian horses. Sir. there is no man in Canada, who loves a good horse, a beautiful horse, much more than I do. I would say of the man who does not love a horse what Shakespeare said of the man who hath not music in his soul. But there is nothing in connection with this Bill that will in any way affect injuriously horses or the lovers of good horses. Men like clean sport, but they do like the sport to be clean; otherwise it is not sport. I claim that race-track gambling does much to deteriorate sport and does nothing to elevate it and that we can have much cleaner and better sport without the gambling. It has been said that we must have men to ride horses, that it is men who are accustomed to riding upon horseback who will be of use to us in time of war and that for the purposes of our militia, for military reasons, it is a good thing to encourage riding. There is nothing in this Bui in any way to discourage riding. A man is permitted to ride, to ride any kind of horse or to hold any kind of race meeting as surely and as freely under this Act as he could do if there was no such Act. But I want to say more, that while horseracing, and especially race-track gambling, has been rapidly increasing in Canada, horse-back riding has been growing less and less common, and that there are in Canada to-day fewer people who ride horseback than there were 50 years ago. As to the manner in which it'may affect the breed of horses, I wish to say that we have in Canada the draught horse which is not affected in any way by any action that may Mr. MILLER.	.
be taken as regards the thoroughbred. We have the hackney, and the trotting horse and the various breeds-of coach horses which are not affected even by horse-racing et alone this Bill, and for the breeding of which thorough-bred or running horses are not used. There are many counties in this Dominion and in every province in Canada where no thoroughbred horses have been used for breeding purposes, not so many are used, I think, as there ought to be. I go further and say that whether for the improvement of trotting, or saddle or riding or any other breed of horses, the thoroughbred used is not the stamp of thoroughbred that is found upon the racetrack.
I was talking a few days ago to a member of this House who loves horses, as many of us do, and who is fond of seeing a good horse-race. Once in a while he adds to the zest of the sport and the relish of the race by putting up a small bet. He is a man of good judgment-by that I do not mean that he always bets on the winning horse, but that he is a man of sufficient self-control not to wager more than he can afford to lose and he may have bet many times without being injured in the slightest degree. He told me that a short time ago, coming up from the Woodbine on the street car, he saw a little boy probably twelve years old, certainly not more than fourteen, who was exultantly exclaiming to every one in the car that he had won $2 on a horse-race. This member said to me that he thought: Is there not, after all, an element of evil in this whole thing and may not the winning of that $2 injure and probably spoil that boy's whole life? I was talking to a prominent Canadian manufacturer who informed me that he had in his office a young man who had held a position of trust in some financial institution. The young man got to playing theraces, and lost a considerable amount. At first he took a small sum of his employer's money and losing it took out another sum to make another bet, hoping to make good his losses, but with the usual result, the book-maker had the best of the contest,. The young man's losses and embezzlements increased until he lost his situation. His father had to make good the money he had lost, the young man was to that extent disgraced and his father, an estimable man, came to my friend, and asked him whether he would not, for kindness sake, take the young man into his office and endeavour to make something of him. He did so. The young man was an estimable fellow, every one liked him, but every fall or spring, when the time of the races at the Woodbine comes around, he becomes uneasy and makes some excuse or other to get off to the Woodbine. This manufacturer stated that last year he secured $50 from one member of the firm, $50 from another person

and $50 from some one else. He went to the races with the usual result, he lost his money. He said that the young man, not only lost money he could not afford to lose, but he unfitted himself for business and, so reduced his value as an employee that his employer would have dismissed him were it not for the sake of his father.
Personally I represent a rural constituency within which no ' horse-racing takes place. I have not the opportunity, whether I would embrace it or not, of watching horse-races or seeing personally much of race-track gambling. But a sad instance came close within my own view. A young man of my own town, more than ordinarily clever, was given a place of considerable trust in Toronto where he handled a good deal of money. He began to play the races, and embezzled the funds of his employer in order that he might bet on the Toronto race track. He was detected and sent to prison for two years. His young wife, a very estimable woman, whom I knew very well, appealed to me to endeavour, if possible, to have her husband liberated because as he had been the bread winner his family were suffering in consequence of his imprisonment. She had two little children to support whom, she laboured with her needle. I appealed to the Minister of Justice, first having said to the young wife that it would be no use to make an appeal, until after one half the time had expired. After that time I appealed to the Minister of Justice who said to me: Much as I would like to meet your wishes, I cannot do so; I do not think it would be in the public interest or in the interest of this young man that he should be set at liberty until he had served the greater part of his two years. His wife told me very pathetically of the endeavours she constantly made to hide from her little children the fact that their father was behind prison bars. You may judge whether it would be possible to hide that fact from her children. Sir, there are other wives, there are other fathers and mothers, there are other children, who are being cursed by the results of racetrack gambling. I ask you, because of the evils resulting to Canada as a nation and the people of Canada economically, morally and every other way, to support the Bill, and I trust it may become law.
Will the hon.. gentleman allow me to put him a question? Did I understand him correctly to say that the object of the Bill is not to suppress betting, but only some forms of race-track gambling?

I am glad that question has been asked. It does endeavour to suppress entirely the business of race-track gambling, but we have carefully avoided any attempt to suppress the making of private bets between private individuals.

Does my hon. friend think it perfectly right for him to make a bet on a horse-race with any one he choses but illegal to make the same bet with the book-maker?

We have not endeavoured to suppress the making of private bets between private individuals for two reasons. There are many of us who do not understand the methods adopted by book-makers and pool sellers and perhaps the hon. gentleman would explain what are these methods, and what are the objectionable features in book-making and pool selling so that we would be in a better position to exercise our judgment in this matter.
I think my hon. friend has an experience in these matters which will enable him to give me pointers.

That is not an answer to my question. It is purely a matter of opinion and conjecture on the part of the hon. gentleman as to whether I have had personal experience or not. I have asked the question for the benefit of members who do not understand book-making and pool selling.

Before the question is put, I should like to offer a few observations. I may say that I did not anticipate that my hon. friend would discuss this measure at this afternoon's session, and consequently am not prepared to go as fully into it as I think it would be my duty to do if I had had sufficient time for preparation. But I would point out that we have in the vicinity of Montreal a very important association connected with racing, and I feel it my duty to offer the House some observations on this measure. There is a point in the remarks of my hon. friend which I think one cannot emphasize too much because the general impression created throughout the country-and it is one which I shared myself to a certain extent-is that those who are pressing this measure are absolutely opposed to betting in any form. My hon. friend, however, has said that there is nothing immoral or wrong in two men on a race-course engaging in any betting operations provided they do not make it a business. I understand from him that a man can go on" a race-course and make

bets with another without doing anything wrong and that there is no intention of legislating against any such transaction, but that the evil is done the moment he makes a bet with a book-maker. If I am wrong, I would like my hon. friend to correct me. The occasion for this Bill has been stated by my hon. friend. It is the invasion into the province of Ontario of American bookmakers.
Not alone the province of Ontario.

Well, all of the western provinces. The fact that book-makers have come from certain states of the Union where book-making has been prohibited, is the occasion of this measure, and that the prohibition of book-making, in the state of New York more particularly, has caused that invasion and that some abuses have resulted. I would like to say, with regard to the province of Quebec and more particularly the race-course I have in view in the immediate vicinity of Montreal, that, so far as I have been able to observe, this invasion has not yet reached us to any appreciable degree. The race-meetings I have attended there and the observations I have made myself and those made by others do not bear out the statement that the bookmakers from the United States have invaded that race-course to such an extent that great abuses have resulted. That is one point I desire to make more particularly as regards the province of Quebec, because my observations do not extend outside of that province. I take it as an admitted fact that the racing of horses has the effect of greatly improving the breed of horses. You cannot improve the breed of horses unless you have trials or tests of speed and endurance, and you cannot have these trials and tests successfully unless you * have prizes and betting, and I will even go the length of saying book-making at any rate has been the result of experience. My hon. friend says that there is nothing in his Bill to prevent these trials and tests. That is true, but on the other hand you cannot have these tests which result in the improvement of horse breeding, without the accompanying prizes, the bets and even upon the race-course the book-maker, in order that that betting may be conducted in such a way as to make the race meeting a success.
I would not like to be understood as approving of abuses, nor as denying that abuses do exist sometimes-even often; nor would I say anything derogatory of the bodies and individuals whom my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) has quoted here as having encouraged the movement intended to bring about this legislation-nothing of that sort by any means. But I say that, in my opinion, we can take it for granted that successful race-meetings cannot possibly be Mr. MONK.
held if betting be prohibited, or even bookmaking; and that without race-meetings conducted as they are in England and as we have conducted them hitherto in this country, you cannot have that encouragement of horse breeding that is absolutely essential not only in my province but throughout the whole country. In the province of Quebec-I wish now to become a little more specific-a number of gentlemen of means and immensely interested in the encouragement of horse-breeding and to whom we in that province are greatly indebted for what they have done in that regard, have at very great expense, organized a race-meeting association. And the kind of encouragement that they have given to horse-breeding, even in the short time for which the association has existed, has produced very good results indeed. Of course, in an association of that kind where a large expenditure is made, they must take means to obtain some return. Hitherto, their returns have been very small indeed; I doubt very much, though I am not authorized or qualified to speak for them, that they have realized any dividend whatever. Their object was the encouragement of horse-breeding and not at all the encouragement of abuses in the way of betting or book-making. They have succeeded in improving the breeding of horses in our province, as can be testified to, I am sure, by our agricultural societies and others who are interested in the promotion of that very important national industry. The government of the province of Quebec have realized this also, and have encouraged that association by giving it a grant. I do not know exactly what the amount of that grant is, but I know that the government have testified publicly to the usefulness of the association by making such a grant. But what is more important-and I call the attention of the government and of my hon. friends who belong to the legal profession particularly to this point-the association is working under a charter granted by the provincial authorities of the province of Quebec. That charter, if I am not mistaken, authorizes fully all the operations of whatever nature which that association is carrying on on the Blue Bonnets race-course in Montreal. The reason I point this out to the government, and to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) particularly, is that it seems to me questionable whether we can, by such legislation as this, interfere with the operations of that association, by declaring criminal operations which they are carrying on under a provincial charter-operations, I would furthermore particularly emphasize, which, if this Bill carries, will have to be interrupted, for I start with the principle that it is impossible successfully to carry on a racing association without allowing

not only betting, which my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) states he does not intend to discountenance, hut also that particular form of betting which is carried on by bookmakers.	*
The question presented to my mind is, can we legislate that association out of existence?-for that would be the practical result, as I believe, of such a law as is here proposed.	I
question very much if there does not appear to be there a very serious conflict of jurisdiction between our own power and the power of the legislature. I am not prepared to discuss that at length. But I remember that the question was raised before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Lamb versus the Bank of Toronto. Lamb was a collector of the provincial revenues, and he was endeavouring to collect a tax imposed upon the banks by the province. The decision which condemned the bank was carried to the Privy Council. I have not the report of the case here, but my recollection is that the members of the Judicial Com' mittee stated that if the legislation of the province imposing the tax upon the bank was of such a nature as to strike at the existence of the hank itself the Privy Council would be prepared to pronounce that legislation ultra vires, but they went on to express the opinion that the province had not intended, nor was it the result of its legislation, to deprive the banks of existence or of the power of carrying on their operations, but merely to impose what appeared upon the surface to be a legitimate tax. In this instance-if I am right in stating that to suppress the book-makers would be to render the holding of race-meetings impossible-you could apply the observation made by the Privy Council that it would be a case of legislating out of existence a body created by the province acting within its jurisdiction, by declaring criminal, an operation which, of course, becomes criminal by its abuse but is not criminal if carried on under proper supervision and in such a way as to prevent abuse. I mention this point, because, so far as I have been able to observe, the abuses which exist in the United States, and which since the prohibition there have resulted in the inundation of the province of Ontario and other provinces by the parties guilty of these abuses, have not become evident in the race-courses in the province of Quebec, at any rate in the racecourse in the vicinity of the city of Montreal. In this case, as was recognized, I believe, in the case of the Sunday Observance Act, the duty of enforcing the criminal law, the administration of criminal justice, is, under our constitution, left to the provinces; and it seems to me right that the application of this proposed Bill, should it become law, should be. left in the hands of the Attorney Genera] of each
province. Thus, the Attorney General of the province of Quebec, should the abuse [DOT] of race-track betting spread to that province and be brought to the notice of the government charged particularly with the administration of the criminal law, could, by proclamation, bring this law into operation in our own province. It seems to me that would be just and fair; because the movement to bring about this legislation has resulted, as my hon. friend . has stated, from the chasing out of the United States, or of certain states, the men who created those abuses, or carried on operations in an abusive manner. Their presence, I think, has not yet been felt in our own province, at any rate, on the race courses in question. Why should the men who originated this association, the men interested in horse-breeding, horsemen of high repute-why should these men, having started that association and gone to considerable expense to establish it in an important centre of our province, where their operations are doing good to agriculture, are improving the breed of horses-
Would my hon. friend allow me a question? Has the association in Quebec a charter to carry on race-track gambling, and if not, how will this Bill interfere with that association, or with its work?
I have not the charter of that association. But I said a moment ago, so far as I know they are empowered under their charter to carry on betting on their race-track in any form.
If the hon. gentleman is not certain of that, I think he is mistaken.'"' The charter means that they may carry on racing but not betting.

I have great difficulty in finding out what my hon. friend means by race-track gambling. I think he said that it was far from his intention to prevent race-track gambling, my hon. friend began with that observation. What he wishes to repress is the abuse by men who make a business of it, the book-makers. But race-track gambling in the sense in which my hon. friend Understands it, is, I think, authorized by, or at any rate can be implied from, the powers granted by this charter in Quebec. I have no doubt that if this law passes, a conflict will arise as to whether the association in question, chartered by the province, cannot independently of that law carry on its operations. What objection, might I ask my hon. friend, has he to the insertion of a clause in this Bill that the Attorneys General of the provinces themselves should have the power of bringing the law into operation in our province, where the abuses he has pointed out have not, so far as I am aware, yet manifested themselves? Why should we

suffer because the province of my hon. friend is at the present moment suffering from those abuses? Why should our legitimate operations be interfered with?

If my hon. friend asks me a question I will answer it. If there are in his province no offenders, the law will not apply; but if in his province there are offenders, then the insertion of anything such as he requests in the Act will make it difficult to enforce the Act.

Of course, in a large city like Montreal, I have seen a great many results of speculation, results that, among young men, are indeed melancholy. But as far as I am personally concerned, I have not seen a young man in Montreal yet, or in the vicinity, who has come to grief in the way my hon. friend explained a moment ago, through betting on race-tracks. I have not yet seen any such case, though I have seen a great many eases of young men falling and being sent to the penitentiary through speculation, gambling of different kinds. But of gambling on race-tracks, I have not seen yet any cases. Of course there are abuses in Montreal, as everywhere else. I have seen abuses in bazaars, in kermesses, in election competitions, carried on even for the erection of churches and other laudable objects. But I have not yet seen on race-courses the abuses to which my hon. friend has referred. They have in France a system of betting in which one is not exposed to make great losses or great gains. I would not like the House to think I am a betting man, because I am not, nor am I familiar with that particular kind of betting which is called Pari-Mutuel. But I know it has been countenanced in France, for the reason, I suppose, that the system is carried on under the control of the state, and as it is a source of gain, the state has distributed such gain for agricultural purposes throughout France. The gains resulting from this Pari-Mutuel amounts to millions of francs every year, and this sum the government distributes for public purposes. I do not know whether it would be possible to introduce that system here which exists in different countries of Europe. But it has that advantage that you cannot lose a great deal nor gain a great deal, according to the principle that you cannot have a proper risk without betting. It might be a good idea for the government to allow the system of PariMutuel to be carried on by the racing authorities under proper supervision.

I am of opinion that this Bill should pass its second reading without prolonged discussion, and should then be referred to a select committee of this House to investigate the whole matter and report.. My hon. friend who introduced the Bill (Mr. Mr. MONK.
Miller) has given an involved legal argument, and I do not think that many members of this House can, by a discussion of these clauses in committee, get at all the abuses that my hon. friend is attempting to suppress. by this Bill. Now, my hon. friend has used the expression, ' Playing the races,' As I understand it, betting upon horse-races takes place every day in the year, and in other places than on the racetracks at actual meetings. But I am of the opinion, although I would not like to be positive, that the greatest abuses in connection with race-track gambling take place in the pool-rooms, or among what are called hand-book operators, betters of that kind. Last night, in taking up the Toronto ' World,' I found on one page nine different advertisements, one of which I will read, as it will give an idea of all the others.

Room i, 21 Leader Lane.
Monday I gave out, Patsy 8 to 1, won. Yesterday I gave out, Woolstone, 3 to 1, won.
Follow me at Jacksonville, boys, and you'll get the money.
To-day-8 to 1-to-day.
This is a sure winner and one that you can go as far as you like on. I have the word to-day that there is no chance to go wrong. Don't miss this one, boys.
That is the purport of nine different advertisements that appear In this paper, and all in the city of Toronto. In the first place, I point out that it mentions Jacksonville. There is a race-meeting going on in Jacksonville at the present time, and that would imply that there are eight or nine concerns, in the city of Toronto, doing business and recording bets, or that there was some sort of betting carried on in -connection with the races at Jacksonville. If that be true, that is something that should be prohibited. I am not sure whether tmy hon. friend's Bill covers cases of that kind or not, but I fully believe that the great abuses that exist in what is called playing the races arise from outside betting, that is the betting that goes on from day to day and year to year, and not the betting that goes on at a properly regulated race-course. I heard an expression about pool-rooms, hand-book operators and that sort of thing. I never was in a pool-room, and I do not know how they are operated or carried on. I have never seen a hand-book operator to my knowledge. I do not know exactly how he carries on his business, but I have been at one race-track in Canada on several occasions, that is the Woodbine at Toronto, and I must say that if no greater abuses exist on the other race-tracks in Canada than what I have been able to see at the Woodbine, I do not see very much cause for this legislation. As I say, I have not very much information on this subject, my

information may be erroneous and that is why I would like to see it go to a special committee of the House in order that we might find out all about the subject and be able to legislate intelligently. Betting with the book-maker on the race-track is a different proposition from betting with a bookmaker in a pool-room or on the street outside of the race-track. If I am correctly informed, when you go into a pool-room the book-maker who conducts the business, or the hand-book makeT, fixes the odds and you are betting upon his judgment entirely and upon such information as he is able to get, but when you go to the race-track and bet against that book-maker the .bookmaker does not make the odds; it is the public that make the odds. Everything is done in the open and above board. It is true that the book-maker produces his slate and suggests the odds, but the public actually make the odds. The book-maker may open the betting on a certain horse at ten to one, but the price is brought down to five to one, or perhaps even money. Why? Because the public take up the proposition and force the price down. So, I say that on the race-track the public make the odds and not the book-maker. If the racing association properly regulates its business, and the association is properly regulated, I do not see any very great, harm in betting on the race-track. I am informed, however, that there are many race-tracks in Canada that do not carry on their business in the same manner as it is carried on at the Woodbine. As to that, I do not know. That is one thing I would like to have investigated by a select committee of the House. I am informed that there are race-tracks that are really owned, controlled and operated by professional gamblers or book-makers. They advertise a race-meeting and carry it on for three or four weeks, or thirty or sixty days, so that they are carrying on at the race-track a similar business to that which they carry on in the pool-rooms. If that be true certainly that class of race-tracks should be regulated. That class of betting on race-tracks should be, in fhy opinion, entirely prohibited. How can that be done? Supposing that some Act were passed to restrict the length of these meetings to a week or ten days and to limit the number of meetings in a year, or something of that sort it would have the effect probably of putting that class of race-tracks out of operation. As far as race-track gambling is concerned the foundation of the thing is the regulation of the race-track associations instead of resorting to the Criminal Code. However, as I say, I am not absolutely certain upon this. I would like to see the question referred to a select committee, so that we could get exact, full and complete information regarding it. If what I have
suggested is true I fear that my hon. friend's Bill will not regulate many abuses, that, I am informed, do exist in certain parts of the country.
Would the hon. gentleman tell me to what particular point he refers now?

Regulating the length of the meetings. I do not see anything in the Bill that at all regulates racing associations. I think that it is the racing associations, the jockey clubs that carry on race meetings and permit gambling upon their premises that should be dealt with first.
I do not think the Bill touches that feature of the case at all and I think that is the first thing that should be dealt with. My hon. friend stated, and it appears in the numerous petitions that have been presented to parliament day after day for the last week, that race-track gambling had been prohibited in Japan and in several of the states of the American Union. They do not say that it has been prohibited in Great Britain, France, Austria, Russia, Italy Australia, New Zealand or in any of those countries in which horse-racing and racetrack betting were in existence long before they were known in the United States. From that I think I have the right to assume that when, in these countries that I have just mentioned, racing associations are in existence and where betting takes place on the race-tracks, they must have some way of regulating them because the evils do. not exist that appear to exist in some of the states and on some of the racetracks in Canada. It may be that in those particular states that have be^en referred to by my hon. friend the race-tracks are controlled by the book-makers or professional gamblers and not by men who are in the business for the sport that is in it. I would judge that from reading this^ advertisement which I have just now given to the House, because these men pretend to get, and perhaps do get, information from Jacksonville as to what horse is going to win on a certain day.
That would lead me to believe that the track at Jacksonville is operated and manipulated by men who are in the gambling business and not actually in the racing business, and probably such was the reason for prohibiting betting in these various states. I believe there are very many strong reasons why this matter should be referred to a special committee of the House. Horse-racing has been called the sport of kings and I suppose there is no country in the world to which that description more aptly applies than our own, so that, if the absolute prohibition of betting would ruin this kingly sport as is alleged it may be well for us to inquire in the matter. I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) that I cannot see very much

' difference-I can see no difference in principle-between private persons betting with one another at a race-track and betting with a book-maker. That is particularly so when you have an even chance with the book-maker. And I maintain that as betting is carried on at the Woodbine you have that even chance. Probably that chance may be modified by the fact that the book-maker has an advantage in that he visits all the races in the country and may be a better judge of the form of the different horses, but at all events he proposes the odds and the people who bet take their chance, and if these race-tracks are properly conducted the public have an equal chance with the book-maker. However, I may be all wrong as to that and so I would like a special committee of the House to consider the matter so that we may know what the conditions are and legislate accordingly. If this Bill should pass its second reading, as I think it ought, I shall move that it be referred to a special committee.

I agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. McColl) that a special committee should be appointed to inquire into the question of race-track gambling, and particularly so as the hon. gentleman who introduced the Bill was unable to explain to us what the abuses were that he asked us to legislate against. When the Bill gets its second reading I shall have much pleasure in seconding the motion that it be referred to a special committee.

In so far as this amendment is intended to remove the inconsistencies in section 227 of the Criminal Code I am in favour of it. Section 227 defines a common betting house as 'a house, place, room, or other place', and the courts in interpreting that section have held that a book-maker in a booth or stall or in a hand wagon run about the inclosure commits an offence under the Criminal Code, but that if he walks about even though he has placards all over him declaring himself to be a book-maker, and even though he uses all the arts of a book-maker, he is not within this section. The courts have gone further and have held that if the book-maker is standing on a chair he is liable to a penalty, but that if he gets down from that chair and walks about he is not committing an offence. It seems to me that the provisions of the Criminal Code should square with our moral sense, and our moral sense teaches us that in the one case the crime is as great as in the other. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) when he says that book-making is a necessary concomitant of races. I believe that the lover of horses needs no such incitement to induce him to take part in clean races, conducted in a clean way, and I believe that when this parliament Mr. McCOLL.
