passed section 227 and gave the definition it did, it really meant to put an end to book-making whether a man stands on a chair, sits in a booth or stall, goes about in a hand wagon, or walks about covered with placards proclaiming himself to be a book-maker. The amendment offered by my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) seems well calculated to remove the anomaly I have referred to and for that reason I shall support it.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I think it is my duty to say a few words in favour of the motion of the hon. member from West Northumberland (Mr. McColl), that this Bill be referred to a special committee.
Without entering upon the merits of this question, and, consequently, without saying what stand I might take should the Bill come back before us, I shall state that the chief motive which urges me in voting for the motion to refer is that, apart from the race track at Blue-Bonnets to which the hon. member from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has alluded, there is also the ' Montreal Driving Club ' at De Lorimier Park. I do not know what goes on in Toronto, on the Woodbine race track, but I am aware of what happens at Blue-Bonnets and at De Lorimier's Park, and I can corroborate what the hon. member from Jacques Cartier has said on this subject.
I am in favour of referring this Bill to a special committee because both the associations I have just mentioned claim that they have provincial charters, and, consequently, that they are entitled to engage in betting transactions. I know that during last summer war was waged against the ' Montreal Driving Club;' one newspaper has even deemed proper to enter upon a crusade against the association. I am not aware that the association has been blamed or has been warned by any magistrate, but I know that the proprietors of the ' Montreal Driving Club ' claim and assert publicly, as they did at that time, in all the Montreal newspapers, that they had the right to act as they did and that matters were left in abeyance.
We are not here to find out new crimes, especially when they relate to actions that the legislatures permit. Thus, in the province of Quebec, the civil code authorizes betting when it tends to the improvement of the breed of horses.
I shall not dilate longer on the subject and, and as already stated, I shall vote for the motion introduced by the hon. member from Northumberland asking that this Bill be referred back to a special committee for consideration and report.

Mr. Speaker, this is a question that does not properly belong to this House. The ad-

dress of my hon. friend is an attack upon the province of Ontario within the jurisdiction of whose legislature this matter properly falls. The province of Ontario is one of the best provinces in this Dominion. Such a charge as has been made against racetrack-gambling by the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) should not be laid in this House. It is a question with which the local legislature of Ontario alone ought to deal. I must say that I have been on the race-track in Toronto once or twice, but I saw nothing at all like what the hon. member describes. He told a most pathetic story about a small boy going home with $2 in his pocket. I saw a bby going home with a dollar in his pocket "and I asked him how he got it. He said that ten little newsboys each put a ticket in a hat and had each put in ten cents and he happened to draw the lucky ticket. The hon. member calls that gambling. There is no gambling about it at all. I know of no race-track in this country that amounts to much escept the Woodbine in Toronto and it is a credit to Canada. We did have a batch of Americans who came over to Fort Erie and set up a race-track and another similar institution was established at Windsor. These men should have been put out of the country. They were not Canadians .and their race-tracks were not desirable, but they should have been dealt with by the government of the province of Ontario, not by this government. If the effect of this Bill would be to do away with gambling in this country I would be glad to support it, but there is other gambling in Canada far worse than race-track gambling which is not affected by this proposed legislation. This Bill, in fact, only touches the fringe of the gambling in Canada. The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) very wisely keeps clear of that. Thousands of petitions have been presented to this" House upon this subject and I have examined many of them. Sir, many of these petitions are signed by young girls who know nothing about the subject and who have never been on a race-track. I am proud to say that I am perhaps the only member of this House who lives in a thoroughly respectable, non-gambling community-I have not received one petition from the city of London on this subject.
Does the hon. member resent having been so neglected by the young ladies of his Tiding?

No, I am pleased to know that our young ladies do not know anything about the gambling evil to which the hon. member has referred this afternoon. I protest against the hon. member's description of a state of things that I hope does not exist in this country; if it does exist it is the legislature of the province of
Ontario who are responsible for this alleged evil, they should right it and not the Dominion of Canada.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, before the House rose at six o'clock, I referred to a small boy having won one dollar by ten of them putting up ten cents each and drawing tickets from a hat. I wish to state that did not take place at the Woodbine track, because the Woodbine course is so well conducted that no small boys such as the member for South Grey referred to are allowed within the grounds. I understand this Bill is likely to go before a special committee, and I do not know that I shall make further remarks but wait the report of that committee, and if that committee can show me that the statements of the hon. member for South Grey are founded on fact, I shall only be too pleased to vote for this Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. MADDIN (South Cape Breton).
speechtext:
I have much pleasure in endorsing this amendment to the Criminal Code introduced by the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller). The view appears to be entertained by a numbeT of hon. gentlemen that horse-racing improves the stock of the country, and that for this reason we should allow horse-racing to be indulged in, because if repressed we would thereby be preventing the improvement of the breed of horses. I do not know how that may be in other provinces, but in the province of Nova Scotia, the horses that usually get away with the money in contested events are brought either directly from the United States to take part in those events or are horses that have been imported from the United States, and very few of the prizewinners are bred in the province. Furthermore, the horses which participate in track events, whether running, trotting or pacing are not such as the people of the country are most deeply interested in. But while supporting this legislation, I would venture with some apprehension, to offer a suggestion to my hon. friend from South Grey, and that is to Temedy what I consider an irregularity in the Bill itself. He has told us that the Bill was drafted by three well known legal gentlemen at the instance of the Reform Association in Canada. Well, if I may be permitted to refer to the law as it originally stood, I would mention that under the common law, in the old country, the business of gambling was prohibited, and in the imperial draft code, when the common law was modified, that prohibition was embodied in certain sections from which the general sections in our Code of

1896 were drafted. Sections 226 and 227 of our Code of 1906 follow verbatim the sections 197 and 198 of the Criminal Code of 1892. Section 226, for instance, defines a common gaming house as a house erected or place kept by any person for gaming. Under the amendment now before the House, the word 'space ' is substituted'for house, and a common gaming place is a place used by any one-the wards ' house, room or ' being struck out and the word ' kept,' which is significant, is changed to ' used.' The same is true with regard to 227. Now the punitive ot penal section 228 in the amendment goes on to say:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to one year's imprisonment who keeps any disorderly house or other disorderly place, that is to say, any common bawdy house, common gaming place, common betting place or common opium joint as hereinbefore defined.
It must be quite apparent that the user of the place is not punished under the penal section of this amendment, and as the law stood under the old sections 226 and 227, as was pointed out by hon. gentlemen on this side before dinner recess, if a person making and registering bets, commonly called a book-maker, carries on his nefarious business within a building, room or generally in some fixed place, then the old sections, as they stood, would reach and punish him, but under the decisions of our court, as pointed out by my hon. friend from South Grey, it was found that a bookmaker who moved around on the grounds and in front of the grand stand amongst the crowd and who moved on, when requested by the police, was not such a one as is contemplated by the Code and could not be punished as keeping a gaming place. This amendment then is to reach bookmakers moving about the race-track ground, and whilst the defining sections 226 and 227 would reach him well enough, the punitive does not. Subsection 2 of section 228 says:
Any one who appears, acts or behaves as master or mistress, or as a person having the care, government or management of any disorderly house, or other disorderly place, shall be termed to be the keeper thereof and shall be liable to be prosecuted and punished as such, although in fact he or she is not the owner or the keeper thereof.
Well, if any one who appears to be the keeper of such a place is the one who is to be punished, it must be quite apparent that a book-maker moving to and fro in front of the grand stand and meeting shows very little appearance of being the keeper, and is in fact not the keeper, and so this Bill would not reach him. I venture the suggestion to my hon. friend from South Grey that he would consider the advisability of Mr. MADDIN.
inserting after the first word ' keeps ' in the thirty-first line of page 2 the words ' or uses ' so that the section will then read:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to one year's imprisonment who keeps or uses any disorderly house or other disorderly place, that is to say, any common bawdy house, common gaming place, common betting place or common opium joint as hereinbefore defined.
If the words ' or uses ' were introduced after the word ' keeps,' that would reach a book-maker on the race-track. Then again it would punish unduly the frequenter of a house of ill-fame, which is not contemplated by this Bill. I would, therefore, recommend that irregularity to the hon. member for South Grey in order that he may prepare an amendment at the third reading of that Bill, or in order that it be submitted to the committee should the Bill go before a committee. So much with regard to the Bill itself.
I submit that the benefits to be derived from horse-racing are not commensurate with the evil consequences which flow from gambling on race-tracks. This Bill is intended to punish book-makers, that is, people who make a business of gambling, whilst it does not pretend to punish a person for gambling itself. The real evil flowing from the book-makers' business is that tricksters and people who pretend to give pointers to those who follow the turf, and also to many who know little or nothing about the turf, publish their pointers and tips and circulate their agents on the racetracks and sell these tips at so much per day with a view to leading the unsophisticated and credulous to believe that they can make money by betting to win without any chance against them. The man who deals in pointers, the tipster, is one of the evils incident to the work of the bookmaker. I submit, further, that the business of the book-maker has the effect of cultivating in the young people of our country the habit of gambling and destroys the true sporting spirit of the rising generation, blunting their sense of sporting morality and fair-play.
Now, I have only to say, in conclusion, that I commend the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) for the manner in which he presented this Bill to the House.. Though he is a layman, I think it is safe to say that no member of the bar on either side of the House could have presented the case with greater ability than did the hon. gentleman. He handled the legal aspect.of the subject with all the skill of a trained student of Blackstone, and the moral aspect almost as well as a Spurgeon or a Moody. I am not sure that the isolated instances of moral degeneration and social dislocation which the hon. member has pictured could fairly be called the outcome of race-track

gambling only. Still, I submit that the evils flowing from the traffic of book-making on the race-tracks of this country are such as to warrant this House in passing this legislation. As pointed out this evening, this legislation is not new. The very acts which will make a person guilty under this amendment would always have made a person guilty under the law as it stood if they had been carried out in any fixed place, under cover, in some room, in one spot. It has now become necessary to enlarge the operation of the criminal law in order to catch the book-maker who has been shrewd enough to discover that by keeping on the move, by abandoning any place of abode or fixed point of operation, he can evade the consequences of his conduct. It is in order to bring home to him the consequences of his crime -that this legislation is sought. I support the measure because I believe it in the best interest of the country and because I believe it is right.

I have listened with great interest to this discussion, and I cannot let the opportunity go by without putting myself on record as absolutely in favour of the amendment of the Criminal Code here proposed. In fact, I know of no question that touches a greater mass of the people than the question of race-track gambling. I think the House cannot pass a better measure during the present session than this, and I hope it will be passed unanimously/ I must congratulate the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) on the exceedingly clear way in which he placed the question before the House. Personally, I would support this measure if for nothing else than because it properly defines the word 'place' under the criminal law. It seems a most peculiar anomaly of the criminal law that a man can act as book-maker wandering around from place to place and be held quite innocent under the law, but the moment he becomes stationary he is liable to punishment. The question at issue, I think, was well put in the judgment of Chief Justice Moss in the Moylett case. Let me read a word from that decision: In speaking of the so called ' place ' in question in this case, he said: There was _ an absence of ' that measure of localization and fixity and exclusive .right of user which is necessary to constitute a place.'
It is to meet this difficulty, as I understand it, that this measure has been brought before the House. I believe that by passing this Bill and thus defining the word ' place ' we would go far to overcome the difficulty which stands in the way of putting a stop to illegitimate race-track gambling in Canada. I do not know the conditions in Quebec or the maritime provinces, but I do know the conditions in the prairie
provinces. Outside of Winnipeg, the race-meets are small, but at every meet there are a number of people who make it their business to follow the race-track-do nothing else. If a man got a fair deal in dealing with book-makers, possibly it would not be of so much importance to pass legislation. But every body knows that the dice are loaded against the person dealing with the book-maker. So far as the portion of the west in which I reside is concerned, every one will be in favour of this amendment. No better legislation could be passed by this House.

I have but a few words to say on this Bill. I wish to go on record as being heartily in support of the measure. I also wish to take exception to a statement of the hon. member (Mr. Miller) who introduced the Bill wherein he represented that there was an extended race-meet in the city of Victoria during the past summer. I call attention to the fact that the meeting was not in my constituency, but in that of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith). At the same time, I am prepared to admit that some gentlemen who reside in my constituency extended a moderate support to that race-meet. But we have had in that constituency an experience of what this business means when carried to the extent to which the people who support it are prepared to carry it. The state of California prohibited betting on race-tracks with the result that we had all the thugs and undesirable characters of the Pacific coast landed on the constituency which I represent for a period of sixty days last summer, and the experience of that town, both commercially and morally was the reverse of satisfactory. I am in hearty support of this measure and will do everything I can to see it carried through.

subtopic: IF SO I AM ON THE SPOT.

speechtext:
I own a stable of horses and am in the know when many a good thing will be cut loose here this winter. I want to put you next when I have them on tap. I don't want any money in advance, merely the winnings of a two-dollar commission on each horse I send you, and they may be one, or two, or even three, a week.
Can I put you on my list?
I will make some money for you.
Send me $2 (two) American money, as a guarantee that you will accept my wires, and we can do business.

326 West Ashley Street, Jacksonville, Florida.
I will not make any further remarks on this question, as it has been already so fully discussed. But I would like to see an amendment introduced to this effect:
That all advertisements soliciting patronage for betting on race-tracks shall be prohibited.

I do not wish this Bill to go through without voicing my sentiments in its favour. So far as this Bill is concerned, or any other Bill calculated to effect moral reform, I am willing to support it. What I object to is that the hon. member who introduced this Bill is willing to allow gambling on one side to be( carried. on, while on the other he wishes people to be prosecuted. I would like to see a Bill carried that would make all kinds of gambling illegal, and render every person engaging in gambling liable to prosecution. Now this matter of gambling restrictions was brought to the attention of the government some time ago, and the Secretary of State, instead of taking it into his consideration and trying to carry out the wishes of the people, was willing to legalize it and give the applicants a Bill that made it legal to do gambling throughout the Dominion of Canada.
May I interrupt my hon. friend? The Secretary of State never did anything of the kind, nor was he asked to do anything of the kind.

I may say that an application was made to the Secretary of State to grant a charter that would legalize gambling in the city of Toronto, and the Secretary of State gave a charter which legalizes gambling in the city of Toronto to-day.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to reiterate my denial that the Secretary of State was asked to issue any charter legalizing gambling, and to assert that he did not do so.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that the Secretary of State issued a charter that, perhaps, does not mention gambling, but it is part of the. law to-day that they can carry on bookmaking under the charter that was issued by the Secretary of State, and which legalizes gambling. But I do not find so much fault with the Secretary of State, because he was a young member of the cabinet; but he took good care to go to the Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada, who was responsible for the whole matter, and the Prime Minister authorized him to issue that charter to make it legal to carry on Mr. ARMSTRONG.
gambling in the city of Toronto. That charter is in existence to-day, and it is a part of the laws of this country that in the city of Toronto they can carry on gambling under a charter issued by the Dominion government, through order of the Prime Minister of Canada. Now, as I say, I would like to see this government pass a law prohibiting gambling of every kind. When the matter came up before the Prime Minister and his government why didn't he suppress that charter? We know that petitions have been pouring in here every day by the hundreds, asking this government to suppress gambling. What did they do in this case? Instead of going to the Minister of Justice and asking him to present a Bill to amend the Criminal Code, the right hon. gentleman hands the matter over to a backbencher and gets him to present the Bill in order to ascertain the feelings of the House before the government acts. Why, Sir, this is one of the most important matters that ever came before this House to improve the morals of this country, and yet the government have not courage to bring in a Bill themselves. Even if they do bring in a Bill, they have to ask one of the backbenchers to present it. So far as I am concerned, so long as this Bill is in the interest of moral reform I am willing to support it.

I dare say it would be better for me if I held my tongue on this occasion. I am vicepresident of that terribly and horribly wicked concern, the Ontario Jockey Club, and I am not ashamed of it. Now I am a man with a large family, and have seen much of young men. I have always had a belief, and it grows stronger as I grow older, that you may restrict but you cannot suppress vice. Nobody who has attended the Woodbine races but can bear testimony to the strong ground the management of that concern takes in trying to make sport clean and decent. The hon. member who introduced this Bill, if I heard him aright, gave as a very melancholy instance a young man who had been contaminated by winning $2 at a race, and I think he gave his age at twelve years. Now, Sir, one of the strongest rules and regulations of the Woodbine is that no boy or girl under eighteen years of age is allowed on the track. That rule has been carried out in the strictest possible manner. I do not believe that any body who has been at the Woo.dbine races for years past has ever seen a boy-of course a boy of sixteen may say he is eighteen-but you absolutely see no children there.

Let me ask the hon. member a question. What is the motive of regulating the age in the case of the Woodbine? Why not permit boys under eighteen under sixteen, down to twelve, even little

children, and girls under sixteen-why prohibit them attending the Woodbine?

Let me ask the hon. member, why do we impose any restrictions at all in a family on young children? Why not permit them to do just as they like? Why exercise any control over a family? Why do a father and mother control their children until they arrive at years of discretion?
May I ask another question?
Order.
Only with the consent of the hon. member who has the floor.
I have no objection.

I have no desire to interrupt the hon. gentleman, I simply want to ask a question for information. In restricting the age of persons going to the race track, is there not an acknowledgment that there is a moral wrong somewhere in the sport?

I do not think it necessary to answer such a question, if he does not see the difference himself. I cannot explain it to the hon. gentleman if he does not know the difference between ten years old and twenty years old. If I could, by my vote and influence, prevent all gambling I would do it very soon, but my experience is that you cannot prevent by Act of parliament many of the evils incident to human nature. The difiieulty that is before the people of Canada to-day, in my mind, is, to a very great extent, that those who are looking after the morals of the country are trying to put those morals on the lines which they think is right by Act of parliament and not by home and church influences. The Woodbine race track has the approval of all men who are more or less familiar with racing and betting, and I think the testimony of all these men will be that it is possibly the best conducted race track in the world-except none. Yet, with all that, if it were possible by Act of parliament, to stop betting I would give my vote and influence to do it to-day and for all time. I have been in very active business for more than forty years. I have come in contact with hundreds and thousands of young men in banks and offices. My experience may.be quite exceptional but I make this statement now that I have never known in, all my experience, of the case of one young man who has gone wrong from betting on the races.
Oh, oh,.

I make that statement. It may not be the experience of others. I also make the statement that there is hardly a day in the week in which I do not come
across cruel, hard cases, not only of boys and of young men but of women who have entangled themselves, lost money and brought themselves and their friends into terrible conditions through gambling in stocks. To-day, all over Canada, there is wild gambling in mining stocks. Flotations are put up at one dollar a share and inducements are held out through every advertising medium in this Country to buy these stocks and make a great amount of money. Perhaps it is not necessary to say it, perhaps it is a hard thing to say, and perhaps it may be a thing for which one should not take credit, but for many years no women speculator has been allowed to do business in my office. I have seen the evil of it and I think that the women are the ones in this country who are to be protected infinitely more than the men and the boys who are referred to more particularly in connection with this Bill. Bank clerks, and clerks in offices buy 10, 20, 30, or 40 shares of mining stock. They go into debt for it and the gambling in that particular class of stocks just now is causing infinite trouble and ruin to hundreds of thousands of people in Canada. Servant girls are brought within the range of this kind of stock transaction. If any one going through the city of Toronto will go to any of the evening newspaper offices during a baseball game or a football match he will see thousands-I am not exaggerating-of young men, mechanics and boys, eagerly awaiting the result. I will venture to say that in connection with the football match played between 'Varsity and the Ottawa Rough Riders in Toronto last Saturday, a match played -as cleanly and as finely as any match could be played, more money was won and lost, not only in Toronto alone but all over Canada, than there was lost or won during any week of the Woodbine races. I say that because I saw in my own office, from friends of the clerks, telegrams from many outside points asking them to put up $10, to put up $50, or to put up some other amount of money-not in a business way-but on one side or the other of that football match. In the ordinary everyday life throughout Ontario there is more money won or lost by women and men at games of bridge every day than is won or lost at the Woodbine in a week.
Not excluding Sundays.

Not excluding Sundays. I felt moved to say a few words in connection with this proposed Bill, and I say now that if that Bill could effect the purpose which is aimed at and could suppress gambling, I would vote and work for it heart and soul. But, I do not believe that it will have any good effect. The Woodbine races have become a social affair in Canada, they naturally attract a good deal of attention, and it

is a very easy and pleasant matter for the reformers to train their guns on that one particular event and make very strong and serious statements in connection with it. I know I shall probably be misunderstood very seriously among my constituents and among many of my friends, hut I have here a letter from the clerk of the Presbytery of Toronto in which he writes to me inclosing many petitions signed in connection with this gambling Bill and also one or two petitions signed in connection with immorality and vice. I know a little bit about the reason for the gambling evil, but I must say that when I read the resolution of the Presbytery about immorality and vice I thought I knew a little of the bad that was going on in Canada and that I was fairly in touch with those who do know it because I do not always attend to business and I take a very serious and keen interest in many things that are not business. Than the Presbytery of Toronto, there is no more able* no more sincere, no more honourable body of men. They are men who want to do their very best for Canada and in the interest of morality, but, I read in this resolution passed for the Presbytery of Toronto:
Whereas habitual, open and notorious adultery, and habitual, open and notorious lewd cohabitation are not unlawful in the present state of the Criminal Code of Canada.
Now, the statement is made by that body:
Whereas many of them living in this disgraceful state, having been driven from the American frontier states, are making their homes on Canadian soil.
That assumes that many of the people of Canada are living in that criminal and disgraceful state and that that class is being added to largely by men and women who are being driven from the American border states to live in Canada because the laws of Canada are more lax and open than the laws of the American states bordering on the Dominion. This resolution goes on:
Whereas our Dominion is in grave peril because of this evil, owing to the inflowing tide of foreign immigration, thus threatening the sanctity of marriage and destroying the home;
Therefore this Presbytery would urge the Dominion parliament to enact such legislation as will protect Canadian society and morals against this great evil.
I, for one, as a Canadian, born here, living here all my life, seeing, I think, the ins and the outs and the good and the bad of a great city-and not only of a great city, btft of most of the outlying districts of Canada-I repudiate absolutely that statement. I do not believe that such a state of things exists. I have written to the reverend gentleman who sends me this letter, saying that I, with many members who have re-Mr. OSLER.
ceived that circular, are astonished and pained at it, and that we believe it is a slur upon the morals and the character of the men and women of Canada. Now, the meeting which passed that resolution, also passed that terrible indictment against racetrack gambling, and if the meeting had only the same information as to race-track gambling that they had with regard to immorality and the social evil, I say they are making much of little and that they are trying to have suppressed by Act of parliament that which can only be suppressed by the moral teaching of the ministers of this country and the mothers and the fathers of the children.

I did not intend to say one word on this subject. I was here to listen, and to listen carefully, to everything that was said against racing in Canada, and I was particularly anxious about the matter, because for a good many years I have been connected with the Hamilton Jockey Club, of which for some years, I was president. I gave careful personal attention to everything connected with that club from top to bottom, and therefore I honestly think I know perhaps more about it than the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) who probably has never been at a race meeting in his life.
He goes to camp meetings.

I do not care where he goes, but I do think it would have been wiser for those who wish some reform in this connection, to have placed the Bill in the charge of a gentleman who can speak of his own knowledge of that which he discusses. I have a great respect for the hon. member (Mr. Miller) as an industrious and indefatigable man in anything which he undertakes, but I always like to hear him when he is talking of something he knows a little about. The hon. gentleman may know something about morals in the abstract, but he is as ignorant as the babe unborn about morals as applied to racing and race-horses. I am sure he w'ill not take any offence when I say so; he will no doubt consider it a compliment. Sir, I have been a member of a jockey club and I am not ashamed to say it. I have watched every act and proceeding of that club, from those of the directors down to those of the men who have conducted what is called ' professional betting ' on the racecourse. I may say that it has been the object of every member of the board of that club, to which I have the honour to belong, to see that everything connected with the Hamilton Jockey Club is conducted in a gentlemanly and honourable manner which would bring the blush of shame to no man's cheek. I am

happy to say here to-night, that I have heard highly respectable men from the United States and from England, express the opinion that there could be no more honourable methods than those adopted by that club, and that everything they did was very very remote, indeed, from the rascality that has been imputed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller). It has been our effort from first to last to stamp out every

evil thing that the hon. member (Mr. Miller) has imputed such a club and to those connected with it. From the day I entered that club, I acted with a view to seeing that nothing was done that could not be published to the world, and that nothing should occur which would cast a shadow of a suspicion on our characters as gentlemen. One broad idea that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) has brought forward here is, that betting is an evil, but he starts out by saying that he does not object to all betting. Betting in the abstract is no sin according to the hon. gentleman, but betting in a particular way is wrong, and I would like to know how much that gentleman knows about the particular sort of betting he objects to. I venture to say he has not the remotest idea about it, and yet he appears here in the parliament of Canada to lecture the people of Canada on their immorality as regards a thing which he knows as much about as he does about the precise question as to whether Dr. Cook or the other gentleman discovered the north pole.
I have been a member of a jockey club for some years, and although a fairly busy man I have given time and attention, without any personal monetary interest, to the supervision of every detail of the Hamilton Jockey Club while I was its president, and I deny what he has charged. That club and every member of it has done everything that could be done by them to put down what is really the mischief, an evil which the hon. gentleman and those whom he represents could have abolished, had they given their attention to it. We have felt that the whole odium of the betting evil is due to a matter with which he does not attempt to deal, that is the maintenance in small shops, barber shops and other small places, of betting places where small wage-earners can wager small sums upon horse-racing, football or any other sport. That evil was known to exist as far back as the passing of Sir John Thompson's Criminal Procedure Act. That, Sir, is the great mischief to-day and it is an evil which is known to every one who chooses to study the subject. The small wage-earner frequents these places, tempted by advertisements such as that read by the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McColl). In these places betting goes on from New Years Day to the 31st of December. That
is the curse of the business, and if the hon. gentleman has thought of the subject he knows it. These people induce clerks and small wage-earners to speculate for a few cents or a few dollars on races that aTe taking place at San Francisco, New Orleans or New York, betting on the advertisements they read in the newspapers. You never see one of these small bettors at a race meeting such as that of the Woodbine or . the Hamilton Jockey Club. To enter the Hamilton Jockey Club would cost them more than they are willing to venture on their bets. Those who attend these race meets are not the class of people touched by this evil. The injury is done to the unfortunate man who is addicted to betting, as a man may be to drinking or smoking or any other habit. Such a man loses his money in thus betting, because the other fellows live upon his bets. These are the cases you will see in the newspaper reports of the police courts of Hamilton, Montreal, or any other city. At any of the great race meets the people you see around you are not of the class for whom the hon. gentleman is appealing. He tells a pitiful cock-and-bull story about a boy twelve years of age who was boasting to some gentlemen in Toronto of what "he had won at the Woodbine. Does the hon. gentleman himself believe that story? I do not. I know that the whole effort of the Hamilton club is to keep such boys out, and even a member of the club, I myself, if I wanted to bring a son of mine ot a daughter of mine under sixteen years of age into that race meeting, could not do it. Yet the hon.. gentleman tells a story about a boy of twelve years of age who had been betting and making money. If the hon. gentleman had been in the habit of attending these meetings, he would not have told such a story. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has properly said that these things are guarded against by the clubs. I have no doubt that the Montreal, Toronto and Hamilton clubs are as anxious to protect the youth of this country against danger of that sort as is the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller). Does he arrogate to himself a greater anxiety for the morality of the youth of Canada than I have, or than the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has? Does he suppose that because I happen to be a member of a jockey club, I am less anxious than he to guard our youth? The only privilege I enjoy as a member is that I have paid out some money to establish the club. I have never received one cent in dividends or in any form from it and I pay the same as any one else to enter	the club
grounds. I have given labour to protecting and advancing the respectability of the club, to keeping it as something worthy of and not a disgrace to

this country. I have given time and labour and paid out my money, and all the reward I have ever received has been to hear a little abuse occasionally from gentlemen who do not know what they are talking about. Sir, we see the King of England, the ruler of this British empire, honoured and respected by every man and woman in the land, running horses at the races in England. What a rascal he must be! Probably he would even offer ot take a bet with a friend. I do not know whether he gets near enough to bet with any one else, but if he did, I think no man would be afraid of the temptation into which he was running, or fear that he was leading boys of twelve to ruin. The trouble they have in England is that there are a lot^ of touts who use the love that the British man has for a good horse and for the best horse of the day, to draw a shilling or two out of some pooT devil who cannot afford to lose it, and the law's there are framed to stamp out that sort of thing. It has been a slow process, but they are always advancing. But here you do not find the gentlemen who are so anxious for reform trying to abolish the real evils or make them impossible. I heard what the hon. member for East Northumberland (Mr. McColl) said as to a certain class of advertisements. There is much more in it than appears on the surface. Few men here can appreciate the amount of money that has been expended by gentlemen whose hearts are in the improvement "of the horses of this country. There is a general impression that these men make fortunes out of this thing. Why, the men that spend the most make the least. There are men who have devoted their whole lives to the improvement of horses and who have never made one dollar. The desire for gain is not what moves them. It is the love of the thing they go in for, just as in the case of a great many people who go into trotting racing for the pleasure of seeing tests of speed between good horses. I do not object in the least to what the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McOoll) has proposed. I should be very sorry to object to any full inquiry into a subject of this kind affecting the moral welfare of the country. I would like nothing better, so far as I am concerned, than to submit every dollar that is invested in the club to which I belong to the impartial investigation of a committee of this House which would honestly decide whether, taking it all in all, there is not good done by horse-racing. I do not want to further occupy the time of the House. I did not intend to say one word, but I speak honestly what is in my own mind from what I know, and I can honestly say this, that if .1 had to go back upon the last ten years in which I have been connected with a jockey
club, and go through them again with the proper sense of what is due the people of this country and the upholding of its morality, I would not hesitate to follow the same course, so far as my connection with the Hamilton Jockey Club is concerned.

I have listened with much interest to the very exhaustive after dinner speech we have just heard from my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). He seems to think that somebody has evil designs on the Hamilton Jockey Club. At least that is the only logical conclusion tp be drawn from his remarks. Well, he entirely misconstrues the purpose of the Bill. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) appears to have a similar impression regarding the Woodbine Club. Let me say that the hon. member for Hamilton is hardly justified in the severe castigation he has given my hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller). Any one who has listened to the very exhaustive argument made by him cannot fail to come to the conclusion that while that hon. gentleman may be a layman, he has given more care and study to the legal side of the case than many legal gentlemen in this House, and presented it in a more masterly manner than many of these legal gentlemen could have done. The hon. members for Hamilton and Toronto take the ground that this Bill is aimed at the respective jockey clubs to which they happen to belong. That is the only logical conclusion to be drawn from their speeches. They practically admit that these jockey clubs would not exist, if these betting arrangements were not allowed. But that is the very thing we find fault with. This Bill does riot say anything about jockey clubs and does not want to put down either the Woodbine or the Hamilton Jockey Clubs. There is nothing in it to prevent these clubs having racing meets unless they are willing to admit that such meets cannot be a success if gambling be not allowed to go on at them. Well, I think that other hon. gentlemen in this House have just as good a right to their views as the hon. members for West Toronto and Hamilton.	Like the hon. member for East Grey I have never lost a dollar in betting on a race-horse, but I think we both know what is going on perhaps as well as the hon. member for Hamilton. He took good care not to make any reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., (Mr. Cowan) who spoke of the influx at those race-meets of American horses and jockeys from California, and what he said can be argued of every race-meet in eastern Canada during the last ten years. At such meets the entries are practically monopolized by American horses and jockeys, and in the great majority of instances there is an arrangement between the jockeys and
book-makers and every race is sold out before it is trotted. Consequently no man is safe who goes there and risks his money.
You need not buy if you do not want to.

My hon. friend says you need not buy unless you chose to, but I ask the best thinking people is it proper that we should allow such institutions in this country, and allow those connected with them to hold out this bait to the people, especially to the younger men? When I say that such a course is not proper, I believe I am voicing the sentiment of the best people in this country. If you take the flood of petitions we have had during the past three or four weeks, you must admit that they mean something. You may say that these petitions are signed by innocent parties who know nothing about race-meets, but I have only to reply that if these institutions were the splendid ones my hon. friend from Hamilton has pictured them to be, it would not be necessary to make any argument against the gambling connected with them. There has been a proposition made this afternoon to refer this Bill to a special committee. That is something with which I have very little to do. My own opinion however, is that if we refer it to a special committee, that will give the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) a chance to bring down the officers of these jockey clubs, and of course they will say there is nothing wrong with these clubs. I do not think that the members of the Canadian House of Commons need the evidence of these gentlemen to inform them whether there is gambling going on at these race-meets or not. Every one here to-night knows that gambling transactions are there taking place. We have as much information on that point to-night as if we were to investigate the matter during months, and I see no reason why we should refer this Bill to a special committee or follow any other course than the one usually pursued. Therefore, I shall vote that this Bill be taken up in the ordinary course and I hope it will pass and become law.

It was not my intention to offer any remarks on this matter; but, as an old sport, I thought that probably-seeing this appears to be a time for a confession of faith on the part of the members of the House-a little of my own experience might do no harm. From my early boyhood, I have been engaged in athletic pports of every description. And I never, directly or indirectly, wagered a farthing on any game in my life. I am not claiming any special virtue for that. All I say is that I was not prevented from doing it by any Act of parliament. Fortunately, I had the training in my home and in my school life 29	'
that taught me that it was not very creditable for a fellow to try to get something for nothing. The virtuous outburst over race-track gambling that we have heard tonight reminds me of two instances in the history of this country. One was .the Sunday Observance law-as great a fake as ever was placed on the statute-book of any land. The gentleman who led in putting that enactment through refused point-blank to make duck-hunting on the Sabbath illegal, but they provided that if a young fellow hired a rig to go and see his best girl he was guilty of a crime. The other incident took place a few years ago in Toronto. The exhibition people there, with the desire of affording those who were inclined to be pleased with the classic in sculpture, organized what they termed 'living pictures'. They picked up a lot of old girls from all over the United States, decked them out in tights and showed them as 'living pictures' at the exhibition. There was a great outcry and the ministerial association of Toronto took the matter up. And, in order to decide whether this thing was moral or immoral, those who were ap-pc inted as a committee went out there day after day. Finally, on the last day of the fair, they reported-well, I really forget how the report ran, but at all events they had enjoyed the exhibition immensely. I do not believe in gambling, but I have read this Bill from start to finish and I do not see that gambling is even attempted to be suppressed by the measure. Book-making is condemned, but gambling is not condemned, and gambling after all is the evil. You start a person gambling for matches in one of these pious games of bridge that are played in home parlours or in church parlours, and it is just as seductive to the youth of our country as to allow a boy to go on the race-track and bet his money on the horses. Now, what is all this agitation for? Why, it is just to let my genial fellow countryman, the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) out of a nice little hole into which he plumped himself during the past year. There was a! little Liberal ring in the city of Toronto, engineered by a very able man connected with some race-track institution in the suburbs. That race-track, owing to offences against decency carried on there, was suppressed by the provincial authorities-and, I believe, very properly suppressed. But these gentlemen said: We will teach this Tory outfit that we have pals at Ottawa. So they came down here, and-I suppose, under the law; I am not questioning the procedure-a charter was granted to this company. Forthwith, there was indignation, and that eminent authority on Christianity, the Toronto 'Globe' came out and demanded-in a moment of weakness-that this charter b.e cancelled. My Irish friend, the Secretary of State, not only stood his ground but went to Toronto to talk it out with them. And it was



delightful to see how the poor old Globe crawled-got under the lid and stayed there for some days until the Secretary of State came back to Ottawa. The next step was to attempt to suppress betting on racetracks all over the country-if gambling on race-tracks in Toronto was to be suppressed, it must be suppressed on racetracks every where. And the pious clergymen-good fellows as a rule; I am not saying a word against them-took up the agitation. But let me say here that if the clergy, instead of trying to govern the people by repression, would follow the lines of education, of building up the individual, there would be less necessity for this racetrack gambling legislation. Well, the ' Globe ' got back in this way, and petitions were hawked about the country for signature. And I asked several splendid fellows in my own county, ' Do you know what all this means? ' Not a man of them could tell me the first thing about it. Thousands of names have been signed to these petitions, but I venture to say that not one out of five hundred of the signers knows the first thing of the history of what he was signing. I want gambling suppressed, whether on the race-track or any where else. At the same time, here in my place in the House I want to place myself on record as believing that this system of governing people by repression is not what has given the nineteenth century the place in history it occupies or that will make the twentieth *century what we hope it will be. We must build up the manhood of the nation, and that repression cannot do. Point, if you can, to any period in history where repression has built up manhood. It cannot be done. It is educational, it is kindly teaching the mother with the child, the father taking his boy by the hand. I have a son -I do not want to bring in my own case but I want to show that I am not afraid to practice what I preach-and I am proud of that boy. He is able to hold his own in any place in which he goes in life. And that boy never was repressed, directly or indirectly, either by his father or by his mother. I resent the effort of any man, in politics or out of politics, to repress me, and I have never sought to repress any man; I have never found it necessary. To my mind, this Bill should be relegated to a committee, in order that we may know what there is in this race-track gambling that should be repressed. I have been at the Woodbine a couple of times, and I have seen young fellows bet their fifty cents or whatever it may be on a horse, sometimes winning, sometimes losing. Whether there was any thing wrong with that I do not say. Let us have the committee suggested by the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McColl) that we may consider what we shall do, not only with race-Mr. HUGHES.
track gambling but with gambling in connection with games of all kinds. Why not consider the gambling in connection with bridge-playing? Why, Sir, in this very city of Ottawa homes- have been wrecked by bridge-playing; whole properties have changed hands and people have been led to ruin through gambling at bridge.
Gambling in bridge is to my mind even more criminal than gambling on a racetrack, because the latter is something for the moment, while the other becomes a craze and is carried to an extreme extent. Let me point out another thing. There was a football match in Toronto last Saturday, and thousands and thousands of young fellows in this city and other parts of the country put up their all on that match and lost. Why is it wrong to bet on a horse-race and right to bet on football? There is another point that I think our hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) might well include in this Bill of his. We frequently find another species of gambling indulged in when a public lecture is advertised, or a football match is advertised, and the admission is placed at a certain figure. The tickets are all corralled up, and when a person wishing to obtain admission and is ready to pay the advertised price, calls for his ticket, he is told: Hand out $4 or $5 or you cannot go through. Possibly1 a thing like that would come under the law regulating combines in restraint of trade, or against increasing the price of commodities. At all events, it is a species of gambling, and to my mind it is more contemptible than gambling on a horse race. Mark you, Mr. Speaker, I am not 'a horse-racd>
gambler; I claim no credit for it, because I never had any inclination for it. I was trained in my infancy by a good mother to believe that there was nothing honourable in it, but that on the contrary it was disi-graeeful to be connected with a horse race. I would therefore make a suggestion to those gentlemen throughout this country, the clergymen, and they are a lot of fine [DOT]fellows, a great many of them, a splendid lot, but they are a little too prone, as I have told them on more than one occasion, to take a crack at the politicians. Now politicians are no better than they should be, but I will say this, that I think the politicians of the parliament of Canada, take both sides-I will include the other side too, although it will bring down the scale a little-I say the politicians in this House will compare favourably with any other class, even the clerical class, in the Dominion of Canada to-day. But I wish here, from my place in the House of Commons, to give a word of suggestion to the clergymen, that splendid lot of fellows in this country, and that is that they should direct their zeal along other lines than the present line. It is so convenient to press\

and to grind people down, to crush somebody, and I would suggest that another plan be taken, that they try to reach these people who are going wrong, to extend to them the right hand of fellowship, and show them a better way of earning money than to indulge in gambling, in the effort to get something for nothing. Let the clergymen develop that feeling in the individual, and in their congregations, and throughout the nation, and there will be no longer any need of laws against race-track gambling or any other laws of that nature. But I would say, and I want this to go on record, that I am opposed to gambling; and if my hon. friend from South Grey will make his Bill cover gambling of all classes, betting in every shape, I will support it heartily. To that end I would be pleased to see it referred to a committee, as suggested by the hon. member for West Northumberland' (Mr. McColl), in order that all the facts irt connection with the matter may .be ascertained.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The subject under discussion is a troublesome one to legislate upon, for the reason, I suppose, that in essence the thing struck at by the Bill under consideration is the making or taking part in a bet. Now the trouble is that the making of a bet is not considered by a large portion of the people of this country to be in itself a crime, and that by this legislation which is now proposed, as by legislation already on our statute-book, you are making by statute that thing a criminal offence which, in the eyes of the average citizen, is not an evil thing. It seems to me an innate propensity of the Anglo-Saxon human being to make a bet, to calculate chances, to take those chances, and to stake his property upon his judgment or his skill. The small boy that plays on the sidewalk in the springtime, stakes his marble against that of his playmate upon his ability to make a shot, and if he misses his shot he loses his property, while if he wins, he pockets the marble of his adversary. When that small boy gets a little older, and is able to make or to borrow money enough to waste, he probably ventures into a larger form of gambling, he probably indulges in the purchase of many thousands of bushels of wheat, or many thousands of pounds of bacon or of pork, which the seller never owned and which the purchaser never meant to buy. He simply makes his bet upon his faith that the price of the commodity he purports to buy will rise in the market. Or perhaps he indulges in some other form of stock gambling. Perhaps he goes to the more legitimate broker and engages in speculation by making what is in all substance a merely theoretical purchase of stock in some well known public 29i
company. It may be a company whose stock, if he bought a hundred scares, would cost him more money than he might ever hope to possess. He lodges with his broker a percentage, he takes his chance upon the price going up or going down. He never sees any certificate for the stock he has bought, in all human probability no such certificate is ever issued by the company the shares of which he purports to be dealing in. If the price goes up he sells, he wins the bet, and his broker pays him the difference. If on the other hand it goes down, he probably loses his deposit. Well, everybody I suppose calls transactions of that kind gambling, and it is merely gratifying the innate propensity of mankind, or of English mankind at any Tate, to make a bet.
But these very gentlemen who have been referred to in the course of the discussion to-day as advocating this measure are, I venture to think, perhaps unconsciously to themselves, engaging in substantially the same sort of business transaction, and considering it an eminently laudable thing for them to do. Suppose I go to a life insurance company and want to obtain a policy of insurance upon my life. What else does the company do but avail itself of its knowledge, by experience or by the experience of others, as to the chances that I will die within a year, and make its bat that I will not so die. They calculate the odds, they know what those odds, in the ordinary experience of mankind, amount to, and they tell me, if you pay us so much money, then, if you die within the twelve months, we will pay many times a larger amount. If I die I win my bet; if I live the year out I lose and the company pockets my money-undertaking on their part that if I live they will renew the bet upon the same terms for the succeeding year, md so it goes through a man's life. Such a contract is' in its essence a contract of wagering, a contract of betting in which each party pits his knowledge, or want of knowledge, upon the chance whether or not that particular man will live for a certain prescribed period. Nobody thinks it is wrong, everybody thinks it is right and laudable and this legislation has the defect, that I think every one must appreciate in it that in substance and essence it is running counter to that all but universal propensity-I think I may very properly call it-on the part of the average man to back his judgment or skill by his money.
Now, the practical question here is, I think, whether indulging to excess in this propensity is a thing to be prohibited, or an evil by reason of which you should seek to prohibit absolutely the whole thing, or is a reason why you should seek to regulate it and to prevent, if you can, the excess. Betting upon a horse-race, or upon any

trial of skill, has been the subject of legislation in the old country for centuries at least. As long ago as the days of the Stuart kings statutes were passed in the United Kingdom upon this subject. Very probably before that time it was a matter of legislation and some forms of betting upon trials or contests of skill, or speed, or strength, were considered at all times by the parliament of Great Britain as perfectly legitimate. When we came in Canada to frame our Criminal Code, which contains the present law on this subject, that condition of the antecedent English criminal law was perfectly understood by the men of that day and perfectly recognized in the legislation which is now in question. A great deal of ridicule has been poured upon this legislation, or upon the interpretation of it which has been made by the courts, on the part of newspapers and public speakers who have advocated some change in the law -ridicule, which, I think, is entirely unfair and unjust. I have been brought up to believe, and I do believe, that law is the perfection of human reason and I think that our law upon this subject, as it has been interpreted and declared by our judges, is not any legitimate subject to ridicule, but that the judges have correctly interpreted that which the legislature, whether wisely or unwisely, some seventeen, years ago deliberately enacted in this House. They wanted to prevent the keeping of common gaming houses; they were not striking at the individual bet, at one man meeting his neighbour, betting with him upon anything he pleased and depositing the money in the hands of a third person as stake-holder. They were not striking at the comparatively harmless bet of a pair of gloves with a lady, or a pound of candy, or some other trifle of that character, but they were striking at the wholesale, promiscuous betting engaged in in public gaming or betting-houses. They accordingly prohibited, under heavy penalties, the keeping of a public gaming-house or place. In section 235 of the Criminal Code they addressed themselves to the wholesale betting, if I may so describe betting by means of pool selling at race-tracks, or upon contests of that character where the parties to the wagering contract do not individually come at all into contact with each other, but where the bet is arranged through intermediaries on either side, and with the aid, perhaps, of the telegraph wires or other apparatus. Accordingly, they declared by section 235 that every one was guilty of an indictable offence, and liable to one years' imprisonment and to a fine not exceeding a thousand dollars, w'ho did one or the other of several different things-used or allowed any part of his premises to be used for the purpose of registering bets or wagers or selling pools; or kept or used in his premises any Mr. AYLESWORTH.
device or apparatus for the purpose of recording bets or selling pools; or became the stake-holder or recorded or registered any bet or wager upon, among other things, the result of any race. In passing that enactment the legislatures of that day saw, as any one must, on considering it, that it would render the stake-holder in not only the ordinary innocent bet between two men, but also the stake-holder in the case of a contest for a prize, liable to the penalty of the Act. At every agricultural fair in the province of Ontario each fall I suppose one of the most attractive features is the speeding of horses in the ring for a prize given to the fastest trotting animal, or given for other contests of speed between horses. The owners compete and it was never intended by this legislation to make the treasurer of the association, who held the prize money, a criminal liable to be sent to jail for his conduct. Accordingly they provided by a subsection that:
The provisions of this section of the Act shall not extend to any person who has become the custodian of any money, property or valuable thing staked to be paid to the winner of any lawful race.
That was the first exception. That exception is swept away by the legislation of my hon. friend. He proposes to re-enact the clause as it stands already on the statute-book, to make it criminal to be in the position of assisting at anything in the nature of a bet upon the result of a race or contest of skill or endurance of man or beast, but does not include the three exceptions which were deliberately put into the Act when it was passed as part of the Criminal Code in 1892. The second exception which was made and which, at the same time, recognized, what I may speak of almost as a standing principle of English law, so great is its age, was that the provisions of this section were not to apply to the owner of any horse engaged in a lawful race. Legislation against betting upon horse races is as old as the Stuarts. In the days of Charles II, in the days of Queen Anne, during the reign of George I and George II, repeated statutes were passed on the subject in England; introduced into Ontario when the law of England as it stood at the date of the meeting of the First Parliament of Upper Canada was adopted as the basis of the law of that province. Under those statutes of^ Charles II, of Anne and of George II, while_ there was illegality declared in the making of bets on certain kinds of races and under certain circumstances, the owner of the animal was not penalized if he bet upon his own horse in a lawful race. It was as if he were contesting for a money prize, for plate, or for any prize that was offered to the speediest animal. And so our parliament in 1892, recognizing that condition of the English law which had then obtained for

one hundred and fifty or two hundred years, made that second exception, that nothing in this enactment was to apply to the owner of any horse engaged in any lawful race. Then came the third exception, as to bets between individuals; and finally the exceptional specially made and deliberately enacted by the parliament of Canada in 1892 in order to protect racing upon the race-tracks of an incorporated association. S
'Nor to any bets made on the race course of an incorporated association during the actual progress of a race meeting'.
The parliament of that day adopted that final exception with its eyes wide open. Sir John Thompson in introducing the Bill, called attention to the effect of the legislation. Mr. Davies-now- Sir Louis Davies of the Supreme Court-pointedly called attention to it by saying: 'It is just as well the committee should understand that we are legalizing betting on a race-course' The Solicitor General of the day took part in the discussion pointing out that the law had always allowed betting on horse-races, and so, with fullest knowledge in 1892, a law was enacted which permitted betting between individuals, or on the race-course of an incorporated association, during the actual progress of a race-meeting. And just here let me pause to say that it was with some astonishment-unless my infirm ears much deceive me-that I heard a few minutes ago my hon. friend from Grenville charging against the Secretary of State that by some administrative act of his, within the last few months he had legalized betting upon race-tracks in Toronto. Why, the Secretary of State had no need to do anything to legalize betting.	My hon.
friend's honoured chieftain, Sir John Thompson had done that in this country years ago. If there is anything improper in betting upon the race-track of an incorporated association during the actual progress of a race-meeting, you must strike at it as my hon. friend from South Grey proposes to strike at it, meeting it squarely by repealing the exception which seventeen years ago was put upon the statute-book.
Now, the question, I take it, for consideration to-night by this House is, whether or no that should be done. It is simply a question of policy. Those who support the institution of the race-track in its legitimate form say, either impliedly or in so many words, that if you prevent betting upon the race-track, if you destroy the revenue to the association which they derive directly from the sale of book-making privileges, and if you also deprive that association of the revenue which indirectly they make out of the circumstance that betting is permitted upon the race-track and out of the attraction which that circumstance affords to many of those who otherwise would not attend, you are going to destroy legitimate racing altogether. Now,
I do not know for myself, whether that is so or not. Several members of this House during the day, seem to have made more or less confession, and perhaps I may do so
too.	I had lived in Toronto before I came down to Ottawa four years ago, I had lived in Toronto within a mile or so of the Woodbine race-track for thirty-five years or more,
I once went with a friend to see what it was like, I did not stay more than an hour because it did not interest me at any rate, and I never was at the Woodbine under any other circumstance. I never won or lost one cent upon a horse-race-I prefer to take my form of gambling with my broker. In these circumstances, I think I am in the position of the ordinary member of this House, of being able to pass impartially upon this question. Certainly I do not claim to be and do not consider I am in any way a champion or an advocate of the race-track or of race-track associations. But I find this state of things: We have had day after day during the few days this House has been in session, hundreds upon hundreds of petitions upon this subject. Every one knows who has had any practical experience, how readily people sign petitions and very possibly too much credence and weight can be given to petitions. But 1 cannot think that all those petitions are meaningless. I have had the honour of presenting a considerable number signed by men from my own county whom I know personally; petitions signed without any regard to the political feeling of the men who sign, but petitions which I see signed by substantial men of the constituency and not, at all events, altogether signed by women and children, even if women and children are to be ignored. These petitions were signed by the sober, serious minded back bone of this country. I do not think that -we can afford to disregard petitions of that sort. I do not think we can close our eyes to the fact that whether or no it is manufactured, or whether or no it is spontaneous, there has grown up and there does exist in this country at the present time, a strong body of public sentiment upon this question. But, while that is to my mind well established, I think it is equally the fact that public sentiment upon the subject is by no means unanimous.
The debate in this House to-day has demonstrated that and we cannot close our eyes to the fact that if this legislation of my hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) would have, in fact, the effect of shutting up such race meetings as those of the Woodbine in Toronto or of the equally beneficial meetings held at Montreal or at Winnipeg or at Hamilton, we should be legislating counter to the sentiments and the views of a great many people who can with all propriety be spoken of as, socially and in every other respect,

among the best people in the community. If we think of the class of people who attend our races, we see among them the highest in the land, and when we know that these race meetings are patronized by people of the best standing, people of repute, people who have the best interests of the country at heart and who would never dream of breaking the law or of doing anything which they thought would work any injury to their fellow man, I think it is a subject upon which we certainly ought not to act without the advantage of all the light we can obtain. For that reason, and just because it would be important to know what the effect of withdrawing the revenue from betting privileges would be upon the race-track meetings of legitimate, incorporated associations, I certainly should favour the course which has been proposed by my hon. friend from West Northumberland (Mr. McColl). It cannot do any harm, the session is young yet, there is ample time and after the special committee has heard both sides of this question, has heard whatever evidence may be offered before it by those who are interested in racing and who want to keep up the breed and the excellence of our horses as well as by those who think that the evils which necessarily attend a race-track meeting are so great that the whole thing ought to be suppressed, we shall be in a much better position to deal with this legislation than we could possibly be at present.
I alluded a little while ago to the ridicule which had been in some quarters poured upon the law and the interpretation of it with regard to the question of its being against the law, an illegal thing, for a man to take a bet in the way of book-making at a race-track if he stood still and not at all illegal if he moved about. Many of the petitions which have been presented to the House have referred to that circumstance as an absurd position of things and they put the fault of it upon the judges and of their work in interpreting this legislation. That, I say is a very unfair thing, unfair to the law and unfair to the judges, and it only needs to be understood to be appreciated. When this legislation was passed in 1892, with the deliberate exception permitting bets made on a race-course of an incorporated association during the actual course of a race meeting, it did not meet the approval of those of our citizens who on principle were opposed to all betting, and it was not long before what was considered a test case was made by prosecuting some one under this provision of the law. It was found impossible to secure a conviction, the case was within the exception. Then the ingenuity of lawyers engaged by those who wanted to stop the betting at racetracks was brought into play and some one conceived the idea of prosecuting the bookmaker who occupied perhaps an upturned Mr. AYLESWORTH.
soap box or stood under an umbrella on the race-track, as the keeper of a common gambling house under the other sections of the Act. That was devised on the part of the godly people. That was an effort on their part to circumvent the legislature and it succeeded to this extent. The court said it does not need four walls or a roof to make a place. The statute prevents any one keeping a common, open gambling house or place, and if he occupies any fixed place, in or on a box, or under a stationary umbrella, any definite fixed location, he may be held to be keeping a common betting place if he holds himself open to the public as a man willing to accept bets from all-comers. Accordingly the law was tortured, if the law ever can be tortured, the law was distorted from the intention of the lawmakers at the instance and upon the argument of those who wanted to repress betting on race-tracks, although it had been deliberately permitted by the legislature seventeen years ago. The next step, of course, on their part, was to attack the man who kept moving about, but the courts said that was going a little too far and they could not say that a man who walked up and down, who was continually on the move, was keeping a common betting house or place even although he was taking bets from every one who would walk along with him. I think then if one remembers how this question has arisen he will acquit our learned judges, who have honestly sought to interpret the law as it was set down for them, from any decision which deserves the ridicule that has been lavished upon it.
I observe in the legislation under discussion that my hon. friend has proposed to get over this last difficulty and, if legislation can do it, to make the man who perambulates about but never stands still for a moment, the keeper of a common betting house, because he takes bets from those who speak with him, and makes bets as he so moves around. The legislation in question proposes, in the second subsection of the second section to define the word ' place ' and it says that the word ' place ' means something that is not a place.
The word ' place,' as used in this section and in the preceding section includes any place, whether inclosed or not and whether it is or is not a fixed place, and whether there is or is not exclusive right of user.
We have all heard the ancient conundrum, ' when is a dog's tail not a dog's tail,' with the answer, ' when it is a-waggin'. It seems to me that this is something of the same sort, when is a place not a place? The definition is that the word ' place ' is to include any place, whether it is or is not a fixed place. Now-to my mind, the Word ' place ' necessarily implies and carries with it the idea of

localization and of definite fixity. I cannot understand a place that is not a fixed place, and I cannot therefore think that the object which the framers of this Bill had in view in endeavouring to get over the decision of the courts I have described, can be accomplished by any juggling with words or verbal trickery such as, it seems to me, with all respect to the draftsman of this Bill, the definition I have referred to, literally amounts to.
Just one word more because of a misunderstanding which possibly exists on the part of my hon. friend who introduced this Bill. I understood him to express the opinion, in answer to the observations of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), that this Bill would not prohibit or affect individual bets between man and man. To my mind that is far from clear. The new section, which is submitted for section 235, in distinct terms, makes it a criminal offence for any man to record a bet, so that if any gentleman, who has made more bets than he can keep in his memory, ventures to take out his pocket diary and make the merest jotting, he would, under the proposed legislation, undoubtedly render himself liable to one year's imnrison-ment and possibly a fine in addition not exceeding a thousand dollars. If the House means to enact such a law, well and good, but it should be pointed out that the whole effect of the proposed legislation is to sweep away the exceptions which were deliberately inserted into our present legislation, when the Code was enacted in 1892.
I sympathize to the fullest extent with the efforts of my hon. friend from South* Grey (Mr. Miller) and those who think with him, to lessen or put an end to the evils of gambling.
