But if their efforts will necessarily and inevitably carry with them thd destruction of property, which is already represented by many hundreds of thousands of dollars in investments of our race track associations if those efforts will necessarily involve the suppression of our racetrack meetings and the encouragement which they give to the improvement of the breed of our horses I should hesitate before supporting any change in the present law; and just because I want information on that head and because it seems to me that information can best be obtained by a reference to a special committee, such as has been suggested, I propose to vote for the second reading of this Bill and then to support the amendment or motion which the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McColl) says. he intends proposing, to refer the Bill to a special committee of this House.

Representing, as I do, a constituency which has a race course, I do not think I would be doing my duty to that constituency were I not to say where
I stand on this question. I am in favour of the principle of the Bill but not in favour of the Bill, as submitted to the House, and I think that the proper course would be to give it a second reading and then send it to a special committee, and in that way obtain information on the subject and hear the different views held regarding it better than we can by following the usual course. It is only fair that those who hold different views should have a chance to come here and give expression to their views. We cannot get too much information on the subject before passing a measure which may have such an important effect on this country, and if the Bill were sent to a special committee and there properly threshed out, we could then vote more intelligently than we can at present.

At this late hour I do not intend to delay the House for more than a few minutes. At the outset let me associate myself with the gentlemen in and out of this House who do not believe that you can legislate morality into the people of this or any other country. At the same time I desire to associate myself also with the members of this House who earnestly and honestly desire to correct or remove what they believe to be a very serious evil. For that reason I am in sympathy with the objects of the Bill which has been introduced by my hon. friend from South Grey. It is my intention to vote for its second reading; and if the hon. member for South Grey approves of its going to a special committee, I shall support a motion to that effect. Permit me to say, Sir, that, in common with other gentlemen in this House, who have been sent here to represent public opinion, I resent the attitude of people who are not members of this House and who declare that this parliament must pass this or that measure of legislation. The members of the House of Commons are the mirror of the public opinion of this country, and I submit that it is not competent for any man or set of men to tell us what legislation we must pass and what we must not. Speaking for myself, I am not affected by any views of that kind either in connection with this or any other measure that may come before this or any other parliament.
Let me refer very briefly to one or two observations that have fallen from hon. gentlemen who have addressed the House. I regret that the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) is not here, as I would like to return him good for evil. My hon. colleague the Minister of Justice has made it unnecessary for me to point out to that hon. gentleman that it was not a charter issued by the Department of the Secretary of State which legalized gambling, as he asserted, in the city of Toronto, but it was

the Criminal Code introduced by the late Sir John Thompson. But the hon. gentleman objected to this Bill for the reason that it is proposed to remove the opportunity to bet or gamble at race-tracks. Therefore, it is a fair deduction- that he favours betting and gambling at these race meets. Yet in the very same breath, he condemns the Secretary of State for having issued a charter which, he claims, legalized that very thing. I commend his consistency to the very serious consideration of his mother's son. Then the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), for whose opinion I have the very greatest respect, drew attention to the fact that the race-meetings at the Woodbine track are conducted in a manner which is entirely proper and regarding which he asserted no criticism could fairly be indulged in. He illustrated what he says took place in connection with other branches of sport in this country by drawing attention to the crowds that assemble to hear the results of football matches and baseball games and ventured the assertion that more money was wagered and lost on a certain game of football in Toronto last week than is wagered and lost in any one week on the Woodbine track. _ As to that, I shall not venture an opinion, but let me draw the attention of the hon. gentleman and of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) to the fact that the attendance at these football games, unlike the attendance at the racetrack meets, which my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier affirms could not be successfully conducted unless betting were permitted. is not marked by the presence of bookmakers or by the practice of betting, and the same can be said of hockey matches. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that at these matches the average attendance is much greater, I venture to say, than the attendance at race meets. What does that prove? It proves that two of our most popular sports are not dependent upon betting for their existence. I submit that the whole case against the Bill of my hon friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) was given away, to use a colloquial phrase, by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr Monk) when he stated that, in his opinion, horse-racing could not be successfully conducted without gambling. Now, my hon. and gallant friend from Victoria and Hali-burton (Mr. Hughes), whom I am sorry not to see m his seat-

Oh, oh.
Mr. MURPHY-whom I am pleased now to see on his way to his seah-referred to a family discussion which took place a few months ago in which the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) figured, and with regard to which it is not necessary for me to give the House any particulars beyond those given Mr. MURPHY.
by my hon. and gallant friend. But let me point out to my hon. friend that the charter of the association in Toronto which he was under the impression had been cancelled by the provincial government because of some improper practices on the track of that association, was not cancelled for any such reason. That charter was cancelled because of non-user-because it had not been used at a time prior to its coming into the hands of the gentlemen who were operating under the charter at the time it was cancelled. And, in this connection, it may be well to point out that the cancellation of that charter illustrates a very important, a vital, difference, between the Provincial Companies' Act and the Dominion Companies' Act. Whereas under the Provincial Companies' Act there is provision for cancelling a charter, there is no such provision under the Dominion Companies' Act. So that the strength of lung and quantity of ink expended in demanding of the Secretary of State the cancellation of the charter that he issued was very uselessly spent. All that might have been saved if the gentlemen who were making the demand had only taken the trouble to look up the law or consult the nearest solicitor.
Now, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth) has pointed out certain features of the Bill which render doubtful the effect it may have in actual practice. These are matters, which, I presume, can all be considered in committee. My hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Maddin) has drawn attention to what may turn out to be a very necessary amendment in subsection 1 of section 228. That also may be considered in committee. I desire to draw the attention of the House to one or two other amendments that may be made in the direction of broadening this Bill and making it extend to a class of the population who have been very vociferous in demanding this legislation. In my estimation, section 235 as amended by my hon. friend does not go quite far enough. This section provides that every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to one year's imprisonment and a fine not exceeding $1,000, who -according to subsection (e) as here proposed :
Advertises, publishes, exhibits, posts up, sells or supplies, or offers to sell or supply, any information relating to pool-selling, hookmaking, betting or wagering.
If it is a crime on the part of the men who do this, I want this section 235, so far as I am concerned, extended to the newspapers that assist in disseminating this information. I am going to propose in committee that after the word ' any ' in the twenty-fifth line, the words ' news or ' be inserted. That line will then read ' news or information.' And I will further propose

in committee that after the word ' wagering ' in the twenty-sixth line, these words be inserted:
Upon any horse-race or other race, fight, game or sport, whether at the time of advertising, publishing, exhibiting, posting up, selling or supplying such news or information such horse-race or other race, fight, game or .sport, has or has not taken place.
I submit that the necessity for this amendment must have been impressed upon every hon. member of this House when listening this afternoon to the extracts read by one of the hon. members on this side and by an hon. member on the other side of the House. I do not intend to offer any further observations at this moment, but when this Bill reaches committee, I shall ask the indulgence of the committee to allow me to have something further to say.
I would ask the hon. member (Mr. Murphy) whether he intends to suppress all news relating to the event, or simply betting news?
The news relating to the events specified in my proposed amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
In the case of railway Bills proposed by private members of the House, I have invariably taken the position that where they affect large vested interests, and where there is difference of opinion it is the duty of the House to afford opportunity for those interests to be heard. I think that is only fair. We are here to legislate not alone for the people whose opinions we endorse, but for all the people. If we were sent to legislate only for those who think as we do, we should have only one kind of legislation-and if hon. members opposite were in power, I fear it might be bad legislation. But I have taken the position in railway Bills- fairly, I think and I intend to take it hereafter, that these Bills should be referred to a committee, not in an unfriendly but in a friendly way, so that the people who are opposed to them can have an opportunity to present their views and so that the members of the House themselves can thus be placed in a better position to judge. I am in sympathy with the Bill of my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) and intend now to vote for the second reading to advance it a step and to get it where we can, perhaps, hew it into better shape. But I am strongly of opinion that, in fairness to all classes, and in line with the view I have held on other Bills introduced by private members where interests are affected, we ought to give those concerned a chance to be heard, and consequently will supDort the motion to refer it to a committee.
So far as betting itself is concerned, I believe that the insanity which pervades a portion of the people of Canada on the question of bridge-whist is training people up to be racing touts and book-makers throughout this and other countries, and that the foundation of much of the trouble >ve shall have from betting in years to come is being laid in the homes of this Dominion in playing bridge-whist and other games for money. So far as the sport of horse-racing itself is concerned, I am guilty of liking it. I would rather own a string of fast horses than be the ruler of any of the smaller countries of the world at least. I see nothing wrong in it, I see every thing good in it. The lover of animals is gener-
Uy a man of broad mind, and a lover of humanity also. I am fond of good horses, and I pretend to know something about good horses, and when I am in the vicinity where men are trying to see which horse will go the fastest, call it a horse-race, or a trial of speed, or what you like, I am there to enjoy it. Nevertheless I am opposed to some of the evils that go with it, gambling to excess, men betting their last cent on these races, and I am in sympathy with the Bill of my hon. friend. But in fairness to all classes I take the position I do on other public Bills, and say that all parties ought to be heard.

I have to thank, in the first place, some members of the House on both sides who said some kindly things of me, much more kindly than I deserve, in connection with my address in favour of this Bill. At this hour of the night J will not keep the House many moments for fear I would lose their good opinion, which I desire to retain for at least 24 hours. I do feel, however, some responsibility in taking charge of a Bill of so great interest to the people of this Dominion. I would like to refer briefly to some remarks made by hon. gentlemen who have spoken in opposition to the Bill. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) was the first one to speak. He said that the evil we are endeavouring to combat has not yet reached the province of Quebec. He is fortunate, and the people of Quebec are fortunate that it has not. But I wish to say that when it does reach Quebec, as it will, the machinery of this Bill, if we pass it, will be all ready at hand. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier said that though they had successful race-meets in the province of Quebec, they are not troubled with the evil of book-making, thus proving by good evidence that racing is possible without bookmaking. I think the hon. gentleman was scarcely fair to his own province, which he would have us believe to be very tolerant with and generous to professional gamblers. I think that his words will create a misapprehension that would not be

complimentary to his own province. He said that a certain racing association within his own riding, I think he referred to the Blue Bonnet race-course, had some privilege in its charter that permitted gambling or betting. Now, Sir, I have looked at the Quebec statutes incorporating the old Bel-air Jockey Club, which was at one time one of the first jockey clubs of the province of Quebec, and find that it gives no permission to its members to gamble or to bet, but it does, on the other hand, give them permission to suppress betting and gambling.
The charter of the present association is much more recent than that by letters patent.

I have turned, not to the charter, but to the Act of incorporation of the more recently incorporated company, that is the Montreal Jockey Club, and the statute, in defining the rights of the jockey club, says:
The club shall not permit any form of gambling to be carried on upon its premises; but this shall not affect wagers upon exercises for promoting skill in the use of arms or upon horse or foot races or other lawful games requiring bodily activity or address within the meaning of the Civil Code.
What is the date of that?

1909. Now the Civil Code of Quebec, speaking of betting says:
There is no right of action for the recovery of any money or anything claimed under a gaming contract or a bet. But if the money or thing have been paid by the losing party he cannot recover it back unless fraud be proved.
The next section says:
Denial of the right of action declared in the preceding article is subject to exception in favour of exercises for_promoting skill in the use of arms and of horse and foot races, and other lawful games which require bodily activity or address.
Nevertheless the court may in its discretion reject the action when the sum demanded appears to be excessive.	.
Now there is no greater right given in the act of incorporating that society, that jockey club, than is given by the Code, and the Code gives no right for professional gambling, or book-making, or anything of the kind, but simply says that there may be betting, and the Bill that is before the House does not in any way seek to prevent betting, as I have repeatedly stated.
Mr. MONK, The Code does not prevent betting.

Neither does it permit it. Now, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier and others coming after him have spoken of lacrosse and football, and they say that Mr. MILLER. *
the Bill I have introduced does not sav anything either about lacrosse or football. It does not particularly. The Bill I have introduced does not, unless it does what I do not mean it to do, prevent betting upon a horse-race; neither does it prevent private betting in connection with a football or a lacrosse match, but it does prevent the business of gambling and book-making, either upon a lacrosse game, a football game or a horse-race. It has been well pointed out by the Secretary of State that football associations and lacrosse associations forbid book-making or anything of the kind upon their grounds, and they have large crowds to witness their games, they get large gate receipts, and they can continue lacrosse and football without selling or permitting to any body the privilege of book-making. If they can do that, I would like to know why the same thing cannot be done with horse-racing. My hon. friend has said, and others have followed him in the same line, that we must have horse-racing in order to improve the breed of horses. I have spoken of that before, and I will not now speak of it at any length save to say this, that the ' Farmers' Advocate,' the leading agricultural paper published in the province of Ontario, and as good an agricultural paper as there is in the Dominion of Canada, wholly devoted to agriculture and stock-breeding, has been loudly clamouring for the passing of just such a Bill as this, and those gentlemen are at least as solicitous to encourage the breeding of good horses as my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier . My hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. McColl) has said that the great evil is the outside betting. Now, I think he will agree with me that the Bill is a good one in so far as that it prevents outside betting. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), the vice-president of the Woodbine association; did not endeavour in any way to deny or lessen the strength of my statement, taken from the Toronto ' Telegram ' that $2,600,000 was placed in the hands of book-makers in the last meet of thirteen days on the Woodbine track. This was not on outside tracks, and was not the outside betting referred to by the member for Northumberland. The hon. member for Northumberland has said that while they have done away with book-making in several states of the union-a majority, I believe, of the states of the union-they have not in Britain, or in Austria, and in some other places. If the abolition of book-making, of professional race-track gambling, is a good thing, must we as Canadians, be the last people in the world to enact such legislation? Must we wait till every other country in the world has so legislated? Sir, 1 am a Briton, I believe a true Briton, but there are many things in Canada that I believe are superior to similar things in

Britain. I believe our temperance legislation in Canada and control of the liquor traffic is vastly ahead of such legislation in Britain, and we have better results on every hand throughout the Dominion. My hon. friend from Northumberland suggested short meets, and in this he has been followed by others. Now, 1 am not seeking to attack horse-racing. I am a lover of horses, and the member for Norhumberland says horse-racing is necessary in order to encourage the breeding of good horses. If horse-racing is necessary to develop a good breed of horses, then surely the more horse-racing we have the better, and it is better that the meet should continue, and that instead of being limited to six days, it should last for ninety days. If horse-racing is going to encourage the breeding of good horses, then the more horse-racing the better. I am not seeking to lessen horse-racing, I am seeking to lessen gambling and gambling has nothing to do with the breeding of horses.
One thing I had thought in listening to the speech of the hon. member for Northumberland; I had thought that he was somewhat conversant with the ways of the race-track until about the last statement that he made. Then he said that the Woodbine is run in such a way that the public have an even chance with the bookmaker. Then I thought that my hon. friend was not so well informed as I had thought he was. Would the American book-makers come every year to the city of Toronto and pay large sums for the privilege of making books on the race course if they meant to give the innocent public an even chance with themselves? The hon. member for London (Mr. Beattie) has said that this is an Ontario matter and that it ought to be left to Ontario to deal with. Contrast that with the statement of his friend and my friend, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Barnard) as to the extent of the evil in British Columbia and in his own city of Victoria. My hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid) is not in his seat. I was going to say to him that he very much hurt my feelings and pierced my very thin skin when he'spoke of me as a back bencher because I sit one seat farther back than he does. But, Sir, it is not for that that I make reference to him. He said, as other members have said to-night, that I did not oppose gambling in the Bill and that I said I had no objection to gambling. I said nothing of the kind. I said nothing to indicate that that was my attitude. I do not practise gambling for two reasons; in the first place, I do not believe in it, and, in the second place, I would be afraid that I would bet on the losing horse. I have given my reasons why I have not attempted to penalize the man who engages in a private bet. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), a gentleman
whom we all respect, has rather ridiculed the statement that I made as to the boy of twelve or fourteen years of age returning from the Woodbine where he had won his $2. That story was not one which had come to my own norice, but the story was told to me by a member of this House who was on the spot, who saw the occurrence, who would sympathize with horse-racing and the race-track and who will, I believe, vote against this Bill, I do not know whether that bet was made on the race-track or whether it was made with the bookmaker off the race-track, but I have no doubt that it was made. The hon. member for West Toronto told us that he is vicepresident of the Woodbine Association. I fancy the member said this for fear that if he did not make the statement it would be on the tongue or in the mind of somebody else, but I am sure that those who know the hon. gentleman would not impute any action that he might take or any word that he might utter to any wrong or unworthy motive. I would not think for a moment, nor would any member of this House, that the hon. gentleman would be influenced in his action or in his words because of any connection that he might have with the Woodbine. I do not think for one single moment that the hon. gentleman ever invested a dollar in the Woodbine for the sake of making money out of it. If he did go into it as a money-making investment and if he lost the whole cost of the Woodbine it would not make any particular difference to a man of his wealth. But, I do say this that a man who is vice-president of the Woodbine Association naturally perforce, unconsciously, it may be, sees the whole matter from a rather different view point that many other people will. A man having the wealth of the hon. member for West Toronto moves in a circle and upon a plane where he naturally does not come in contact, as other people with less means and different associations do, with the evil results of race track gambling. The hon. gentleman is not any better qualified to judge of the evils of race-track gambling than I am simply because he is vice-president of that association. He has said that this Bill does not provide a penalty to deal with mining stocks and that it does not deal with the playing of bridge. If the hon. gentleman thought that I was going to concoct some sort of a patent medicine for the remedy of every evil man can think of and if I have not endeavoured to prevent the evil of bridge or gambling in stocks it is no reason why the hon. gentleman should oppose this Bill before the House. It may be his duty to introduce a Bill preventing the playing of bridge and preventing stock gambling and if he does I will be glad, for one, to give his Bill my very careful and honest consideration.
The hon. gentleman has said that many women gamble in stocks, and that women

ought to be protected rather than the men whom we are seeking to protect by the Bill before the House. He spoke of the housemaids who invest their money in mining stocks. I want to know which woman is in greater need of protection-the housemaid who earns her $10, or $12, or $15 a month and then invests some of it unwisely in mining stocks, with no family to support and no children dependent upon her, or the wife of the wage earner who invests his wages at the race-track and, losing them, reduces his wife to want and his children to disgrace. The hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Barker), president of the Hamilton Jockey Club, thinks his knowledge of race-track gambling superior to my own. I admit his superior knowledge. I did not take any offence at anything he said respecting myself. I admire the hon. gentleman so much that nothing he would say, I think, could offend me. But, I say to him as I say to the hon. member for West Toronto that while these gentlemen, connected with racing-tracks and associations as they are, no doubt have honestly endeavoured to engage in the sport as gentlemen should do, and while they may not be responsible in other respects for the evils that attend race-track gambling, they and other men who have an official connection with a racing association have this responsibility that they sell and sell for gain and sell as a means of maintaining their race-tracks the privilege to men to make books. For this we will at any rate held them responsible. The hon. member for East Hamilton has told us of their efforts to keep the race-track clean, but he has not given us any evidence at all of the success of those efforts. The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) speaks of the petitions that have come before this House, that I thought, was well replied to by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice. I had thought that we ought to pay a great deal of attention to these petitions, and that for the most part the people who had signed them knew what they were doing, but I have often thought that the voters in Victoria and Halburton must be a peculiar people. The hon. gentleman says that hundreds of people in his riding had signed these petitions without understanding what they had signed. I think they must have been in the same mood and had the same dazed understanding election after election when they marked their ballots for the hon. gentleman. The Minister of Justice has said that there is, in many transactions, the element of gambling. He said that when a man insures his life or property with an insurance company or association it is a gamble. Sir, there is-absolutely no parallel between the man who insures his life or his property and the man who bets upon the race-track. The man who insures his life gets his policy of Mr. MILLER.
life insurance, the man who insures his barn, or his stock of merchandise, gets his policy and the moment he gets his policy he gets some value for the money he has invested. He gets protection the very moment he pays his money and makes his contract. What protection, what thing of value does a man get who invests his money with a book-maker on the racetrack? I say again there is no parallel at all between the two cases. The Minister of Justice rather conveyed the idea that this Act would penalize the treasurer of any society, for instance an agricultural society who would pay a prize to the owner of a horse. I do not so understand the Act, but I bow to the superior wisdom and great legal learning of the Minister of Justice which we all admire and in which we all have a great deal of confidence. I do not think the Act penalizes the owner of a horse who bets on his own horse. The Act does not mention the owner of a horse, the owner of a horse is at liberty to bet on his own horse or on any other man's horse, but he is not permitted, whether he be the owner of a horse or not, to engage in the business of book-making or in the business of gambling.
The Minister of Justice has said that if this Bill would cause the loss of many thousands of dollars that are invested in racetracks and in racing associations, it would be a matter that would deserve our very serious consideration. Sir, I do not consider, and I do not think this House ought to consider this matter for one single moment; I do not think it has anything to do with the matter before us. If these gentlemen have invested their thousands of dollars for the purpose of perpetuating horse-racing, then I say I have no quarrel with them and I do not endeavour to inter-' fere with their horse-racing-they can carry it on every day in the week except on Sunday, which is forbidden. But, if they have invested their money to carry on a system of gambling then I do not care how much money they have invested it ought not to be perpetuated. Some one has very tersely said that this whole matter is a question of the horse-race versus the human race and if that be so, I, Sir, will endeavour to be the humble champion of the human race. It has been suggested that this Bill be sent to a select committee, and to this I have no objection. I believe I have a very excellent case, I believe that those who with me support the Bill have an excellent case; I am not afraid of all the inquiry that can be made, I am not afraid! of all the evidence that may be produced, and I am willing that it should be referred to a special committee. But I do ask that that shall not be the means of shelving the Bill, I do ask that if it is referred to a select committee, that the committee will act with reasonable promptness so that they may report to the

House in time to have this Bill become law in such shape as it will be agreed upon.
Motion (Mr. Miller) agreed to, and Bill read a second time.

As I intimated, I shall now move that this Bill be referred to a special committee of the House. In selecting that committee I have thought that every portion of the country shall be represented. I have in no sense considered it a party question and have consequently selected an equal number of members from each political party. Then, as there are legal questions involved, I have selected a number of legal gentlemen and I have thought further that members composing that committee should be selected from those particular localities in which they have jockey clubs and racing associations as these gentlemen would be more likely to know the conditions actually existing. As, for instance, one of the British Columbia members spoke of the position of affairs in his part of the country and I have consequently named him on the committee. I therefore move, seconded by Dr. Black:
That Bill (No. 6) 'to amend the Criminal Code be referred to a select committee of this House composed as follows:-Messrs. Miller, Bristol, Macdonell, Monk, Gervais, Barker, German, Lalor, Harris, Clarke (Essex), Haggart (Winnipeg), Campbell, Neely, Barnard, Macdonald and the mover.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, I am sorry to say to my hon. friend, (Mr. McColl) that I cannot agree to the composition of his committee. The committee proposed by him is too large. It ought to be composed of not more than seven members so that it may be a business committee to work a prompt solution of the problem which is referred to it. If we had such a large committee as that I am afraid that the anticipation of my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) might not be realized and that the Bill might not receive proper treatment. I therefore beg to move as an amendment:
That the committee be composed of seven members, namely: Messrs. Miller, McColl (Northumberland), Monk, Blain, Sinclair Stratton and Martin (Regina).

Amendment agreed to.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?

Mr. FIELDING Unless they can be got through more rapidly than usual.
